title: Google Professional Machine Learning Engineer
realWorldValue: The PMLE-2025 validates advanced skills in designing, building, and productionizing ML models on Google Cloud. It covers the full ML lifecycle - from low-code approaches with BigQuery ML and AutoML, through custom training with Vertex AI and distributed frameworks, to deploying, scaling, and monitoring production ML systems responsibly.

skills: 1.1.1: Building the appropriate BigQuery ML model based on the business problem, including linear and binary classification, regression, time-series, matrix factorization, boosted trees, and autoencoders.
questions.question:
The merchandising team at a national retailer maintains three years of weekly sales data in BigQuery and needs to forecast unit sales for each SKU over the next 13 weeks. The data scientists want to stay inside BigQuery so business analysts can query the predictions through standard SQL. Hyperparameter tuning effort should be minimal because dozens of SKU groups must be retrained nightly.

Which BigQuery ML model type is the MOST suitable choice for this workload?

choices.text: Create an ARIMA_PLUS time-series model and use the time_series_id_col option to forecast multiple SKUs in a single training job.
choices.explanation: ARIMA_PLUS auto-tunes seasonality and trend components and supports per-key forecasting through time_series_id_col.

choices.text: Create a BOOSTED_TREE_REGRESSOR model and feed engineered lag features per SKU to predict the next 13 weekly values.
choices.explanation: Boosted trees can model regression but require manual lag feature engineering and do not natively produce multi-horizon forecasts.

choices.text: Create a LINEAR_REG model with week-of-year and SKU one-hot encodings and use ML.PREDICT for each future week.
choices.explanation: Linear regression cannot capture autocorrelation or complex seasonality without substantial feature engineering for every SKU.

choices.text: Create a MATRIX_FACTORIZATION model treating SKU and week as the two dimensions to project future demand.
choices.explanation: Matrix factorization is intended for recommender systems based on user-item interactions, not for forecasting future time steps.

questions.tip: Look at the temporal nature of the target and the desire to avoid manual feature engineering.
questions.explanation:
BigQuery ML offers a dedicated forecasting model that handles trend, seasonality, and holiday effects automatically.

**Why it works:** ARIMA_PLUS with time_series_id_col fits one model per series in a single CREATE MODEL statement and exposes ML.FORECAST for horizon predictions, satisfying the SQL-only and low-tuning requirements.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Boosted tree regressor: requires hand-crafted lag and seasonal features per SKU.
- Linear regression: cannot natively represent autocorrelation or evolving seasonality.
- Matrix factorization: targets recommendation problems rather than future-period forecasting.

skills: 1.1.1: Building the appropriate BigQuery ML model based on the business problem, including linear and binary classification, regression, time-series, matrix factorization, boosted trees, and autoencoders.
questions.question:
A streaming media company stores billions of user-video watch events in BigQuery and wants to recommend videos that each user is likely to watch next. The data engineering team prefers a SQL-driven approach so they can join the recommendations directly with the catalog table.

Which BigQuery ML model type best fits this recommendation use case?

choices.text: Create a MATRIX_FACTORIZATION model with user_col and item_col set to the user and video identifiers, training on implicit feedback weighted by watch time.
choices.explanation: Matrix factorization in BigQuery ML is purpose-built for collaborative filtering with explicit or implicit feedback.

choices.text: Create a LOGISTIC_REG binary classifier predicting whether a user will watch any given video next.
choices.explanation: Logistic regression would require generating negative samples for every user-video pair and would not scale to billions of pairs.

choices.text: Create a KMEANS clustering model on user watch histories and recommend the most popular videos within each cluster.
choices.explanation: Cluster-popularity recommendations are coarse and cannot personalize beyond cluster membership.

choices.text: Create an AUTOENCODER model on video features and rank videos by reconstruction error per user.
choices.explanation: Autoencoders learn anomaly or dense embeddings, but reconstruction error is not a recommendation score for unseen users.

questions.tip: Consider which algorithm directly models user-item interactions.
questions.explanation:
Recommendation problems based on implicit feedback are a textbook fit for matrix factorization in BigQuery ML.

**Why it works:** MATRIX_FACTORIZATION learns latent embeddings for users and items so the dot product yields a personalized score, and BigQuery ML supports implicit feedback weighting natively.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Logistic regression: enumerating user-video pairs is infeasible at this scale.
- KMeans: produces only cluster-level popularity, losing personalization.
- Autoencoder: designed for anomaly detection or representation learning, not ranking unseen items per user.

skills: 1.1.1: Building the appropriate BigQuery ML model based on the business problem, including linear and binary classification, regression, time-series, matrix factorization, boosted trees, and autoencoders.
questions.question:
A fintech company wants to detect whether a credit card transaction will be charged back. The training table holds 200 million labeled rows with mixed numeric and categorical features, and class balance is roughly 1 percent positive. The team needs strong tabular accuracy and the ability to inspect feature importance.

Which TWO actions are appropriate when designing the BigQuery ML solution?

choices.text: Use CREATE MODEL with model_type='BOOSTED_TREE_CLASSIFIER' and set auto_class_weights=TRUE to address the class imbalance.
choices.explanation: Boosted trees are well suited for tabular classification, and auto_class_weights compensates for skewed labels.

choices.text: After training, call ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN or ML.FEATURE_IMPORTANCE on the model to surface feature contributions.
choices.explanation: Boosted tree models in BigQuery ML expose built-in global explainability and feature importance functions.

choices.text: Use model_type='AUTOENCODER' and flag any transaction with high reconstruction error as a likely chargeback.
choices.explanation: Autoencoders are unsupervised anomaly detectors and ignore the labeled chargeback signal already collected.

choices.text: Use model_type='MATRIX_FACTORIZATION' with cardholder and merchant columns to score each transaction.
choices.explanation: Matrix factorization is for recommender ranking, not binary fraud classification.

choices.text: Use model_type='LINEAR_REG' and threshold the predicted score at 0.5 to label chargebacks.
choices.explanation: Linear regression is not a classifier and does not produce calibrated class probabilities for thresholding.

questions.tip: Match the supervised binary problem to a model that supports it natively and provides explainability.
questions.explanation:
The team has labels, mixed feature types, and an explainability requirement, all of which point to a gradient-boosted tree classifier.

**Why it works:** BOOSTED_TREE_CLASSIFIER handles heterogeneous tabular data, and BigQuery ML offers ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN and ML.FEATURE_IMPORTANCE for the boosted tree family.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Autoencoder approach: ignores labels and conflates anomalies with fraud.
- Matrix factorization: solves recommendation, not classification.
- Linear regression with threshold: lacks proper classification semantics and class-imbalance handling.

skills: 1.1.2: Performing feature engineering or feature selection by using BigQuery ML.
questions.question:
During a model refresh, the data science team realizes that their BigQuery ML logistic regression model behaves inconsistently when scoring new data because the same feature transformations they wrote in the training query are not always reapplied at prediction time. They want a way to package the preprocessing alongside the model so ML.PREDICT applies it automatically.

What is the BEST way to achieve this in BigQuery ML?

choices.text: Wrap the engineered columns in a TRANSFORM clause inside the CREATE MODEL statement so BigQuery ML stores and reapplies the transformations during prediction.
choices.explanation: The TRANSFORM clause persists feature transformations with the model and reapplies them automatically at inference.

choices.text: Save the SQL transformation logic in a stored procedure and require all callers of ML.PREDICT to invoke the procedure first.
choices.explanation: Manual procedure calls are easy to bypass and do not couple the transformations to the model artifact.

choices.text: Materialize a feature table with the transformations baked in and grant read access to all consumers before scoring.
choices.explanation: A materialized feature table still leaves prediction-time logic to the caller and risks training-serving skew.

choices.text: Export the model to Vertex AI and add a Dataflow preprocessing job in front of the endpoint.
choices.explanation: Adding Dataflow plus Vertex AI is unnecessary when BigQuery ML can attach transformations to the model itself.

questions.tip: Look for a feature that fuses preprocessing and model artifact into one object.
questions.explanation:
BigQuery ML supports embedding feature engineering directly into the model definition.

**Why it works:** A TRANSFORM clause stores the feature expressions inside the model so ML.PREDICT and ML.EVALUATE automatically apply the same logic, eliminating training-serving skew.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Stored procedure: relies on convention and callers can skip it.
- Materialized feature table: still requires the caller to use the right table and columns.
- Export to Vertex AI plus Dataflow: introduces unrelated infrastructure when the requirement is purely SQL-based.

skills: 1.1.2: Performing feature engineering or feature selection by using BigQuery ML.
questions.question:
An analytics team is training a regression model in BigQuery ML to predict housing prices. One feature, lot_size_sqft, has a heavy right-tail distribution that is hurting model fit. They want a built-in BigQuery ML transformation that bins the values into discrete groups based on quantiles so the model can learn non-linear relationships.

Which preprocessing function should they apply inside the TRANSFORM clause?

choices.text: ML.QUANTILE_BUCKETIZE on lot_size_sqft with the desired number of quantile boundaries.
choices.explanation: ML.QUANTILE_BUCKETIZE divides a numeric feature into bins delimited by sample quantiles.

choices.text: ML.STANDARD_SCALER on lot_size_sqft to remove the mean and divide by the standard deviation.
choices.explanation: Standard scaling preserves the original distribution and does not create discrete bins.

choices.text: ML.MIN_MAX_SCALER on lot_size_sqft to compress values into the 0-to-1 range.
choices.explanation: Min-max scaling is a linear rescaling and cannot represent non-linear effects.

choices.text: ML.FEATURE_CROSS combining lot_size_sqft with itself to capture polynomial effects.
choices.explanation: Feature crosses operate on categorical inputs and are not suited for binning a single continuous variable.

questions.tip: Match the requirement, quantile-based binning, to the matching preprocessing primitive.
questions.explanation:
BigQuery ML ships with built-in preprocessing functions that can be used inside a TRANSFORM clause.

**Why it works:** ML.QUANTILE_BUCKETIZE buckets a numeric column at specified quantile boundaries, producing a categorical feature that captures non-linear effects of skewed data.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Standard scaler: rescales but does not bin.
- Min-max scaler: linear normalization, not binning.
- Feature cross: requires categorical inputs and addresses interactions, not univariate non-linearity.

skills: 1.1.2: Performing feature engineering or feature selection by using BigQuery ML.
questions.question:
The marketing analytics team has trained a BigQuery ML boosted tree classifier on dozens of candidate features and wants to prune low-value features before re-training to reduce cost and improve interpretability.

Which TWO BigQuery ML capabilities help them perform feature selection?

choices.text: Call ML.FEATURE_IMPORTANCE on the trained boosted tree model to rank features by their contribution and drop those at the bottom.
choices.explanation: ML.FEATURE_IMPORTANCE provides per-feature gain scores for tree-based models.

choices.text: Use ENABLE_GLOBAL_EXPLAIN=TRUE during training and query ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN to inspect aggregated Shapley-style attributions across the dataset.
choices.explanation: Global explanations summarize each feature's overall influence and support feature selection decisions.

choices.text: Run ML.PREDICT with each feature individually omitted and pick whichever single run produced the lowest prediction count.
choices.explanation: Prediction counts do not measure feature value, and the comparison logic is not meaningful.

choices.text: Add an L2 regularization term and assume features whose coefficients exceed 0.5 are unimportant.
choices.explanation: L2 shrinks coefficients but does not zero them out, and a static threshold is not a valid selection rule.

choices.text: Convert all features to STRING with CAST and let BigQuery ML automatically discard duplicates.
choices.explanation: Casting changes data types but does not perform feature selection, and BigQuery ML does not automatically discard duplicates.

questions.tip: Look for explainability tools that quantify per-feature contribution.
questions.explanation:
BigQuery ML offers explanation functions that quantify feature contributions and inform pruning decisions.

**Why it works:** ML.FEATURE_IMPORTANCE returns per-feature gain for tree models, and enabling global explain produces aggregated Shapley-style attributions through ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN. Both can be used to drop low-impact features before retraining.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Per-feature ML.PREDICT counts: prediction volume does not measure feature value.
- L2 with arbitrary threshold: regularization does not zero coefficients, and 0.5 has no special meaning.
- Casting to STRING: does not select features and BigQuery ML does not deduplicate features automatically.

skills: 1.1.2: Performing feature engineering or feature selection by using BigQuery ML.
questions.question: Arrange the following steps in the correct order to build a BigQuery ML model with embedded feature engineering and verified feature importance.

choices.text: Profile the source table with SQL aggregations to understand distributions and identify candidate features.
choices.explanation: Exploratory profiling informs which transformations and features are needed.

choices.text: Author a CREATE MODEL statement that uses a TRANSFORM clause to bucketize, scale, or cross the chosen features.
choices.explanation: TRANSFORM packages preprocessing into the model definition.

choices.text: Train the model and call ML.FEATURE_IMPORTANCE or ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN to evaluate each feature's contribution.
choices.explanation: Explanation functions quantify the value of each feature.

choices.text: Re-create the model omitting low-impact features and validate metrics with ML.EVALUATE.
choices.explanation: Refining the feature set and validating with ML.EVALUATE confirms the simplification did not hurt accuracy.

questions.tip: Think about exploring data, embedding transformations, measuring contribution, then simplifying.
questions.explanation: Effective feature engineering in BigQuery ML follows a profile, transform, evaluate, and refine cycle so that the final model is both accurate and parsimonious.

skills: 1.1.3: Generating predictions by using BigQuery ML.
questions.question:
The marketing analytics group has trained a logistic regression model in BigQuery ML to predict customer churn. They now want to score the entire customers table nightly and write the predicted probability and class label back to a results table that downstream dashboards consume.

Which approach should they use?

choices.text: Run a scheduled query that uses ML.PREDICT against the model with a SELECT over the customers table and writes the result with INSERT or CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE.
choices.explanation: ML.PREDICT inside a scheduled query is the native BigQuery ML pattern for batch scoring back into BigQuery.

choices.text: Export the model to Cloud Storage and run a Dataflow batch pipeline that loads it and writes predictions back to BigQuery.
choices.explanation: Exporting and running Dataflow adds infrastructure that is unnecessary when ML.PREDICT runs natively.

choices.text: Deploy the model to a Vertex AI online endpoint and have a Cloud Run job iterate row-by-row over the customers table.
choices.explanation: Online endpoints are designed for low-latency requests, not nightly batch scoring of an entire table.

choices.text: Use the BigQuery Storage Read API to stream data into a Python notebook and call the model client side.
choices.explanation: Pulling all rows to a notebook is slow, fragile, and avoids the in-database scoring that BigQuery ML provides.

questions.tip: Recall the in-database function for batch scoring in BigQuery ML.
questions.explanation:
BigQuery ML supports batch scoring with a single SQL function that runs entirely inside BigQuery.

**Why it works:** ML.PREDICT executes alongside a SELECT over the source table and the result can be persisted by a scheduled query into a results table the dashboards read.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Dataflow with exported model: adds operational overhead with no benefit for in-warehouse scoring.
- Vertex AI online endpoint: optimized for per-request latency, not table-wide nightly batches.
- Notebook with Storage Read API: shifts compute and data movement out of BigQuery unnecessarily.

skills: 1.1.3: Generating predictions by using BigQuery ML.
questions.question:
Following a board decision to add transparency to model decisions, the data science team must produce per-row feature attributions for every prediction served by their BigQuery ML boosted tree classifier. The attributions should be written to BigQuery alongside the predicted class.

Which BigQuery ML function provides this output with the LEAST additional engineering effort?

choices.text: Call ML.EXPLAIN_PREDICT against the model so each row receives a prediction and an array of per-feature attributions.
choices.explanation: ML.EXPLAIN_PREDICT returns predictions plus per-row Shapley-style attributions in a single call.

choices.text: Call ML.PREDICT and then run a separate ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN query, joining the results by row.
choices.explanation: ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN aggregates attributions across the dataset and does not provide per-row explanations.

choices.text: Export the model to Vertex AI and enable Vertex Explainable AI on a batch prediction job.
choices.explanation: Exporting to Vertex AI works but introduces additional infrastructure and data movement.

choices.text: Call ML.PREDICT and approximate attributions by perturbing each input feature one at a time in subsequent queries.
choices.explanation: Manual perturbation is computationally expensive and not a built-in capability.

questions.tip: Identify the BigQuery ML function that returns predictions plus per-row attributions in one call.
questions.explanation:
BigQuery ML offers a single function dedicated to explainable predictions.

**Why it works:** ML.EXPLAIN_PREDICT runs the model and emits per-row feature attributions side by side with the predicted value, no additional tooling required.

**Why the others don't work:**
- ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN: provides only aggregate, not per-row, attributions.
- Vertex AI export with Explainable AI: capable but not the lowest-effort option.
- Manual perturbation: laborious and not a native feature.

skills: 1.1.3: Generating predictions by using BigQuery ML.
questions.question:
The supply chain team has trained an ARIMA_PLUS time-series model in BigQuery ML and now needs to generate weekly demand forecasts with confidence intervals for the next 26 weeks. The forecasts should be persisted to a table for downstream Looker dashboards.

Which TWO actions correctly produce the forecasts?

choices.text: Call ML.FORECAST on the trained model passing STRUCT(26 AS horizon, 0.95 AS confidence_level) to produce 26 future periods with intervals.
choices.explanation: ML.FORECAST is the dedicated forecasting function for ARIMA_PLUS models and accepts horizon and confidence_level parameters.

choices.text: Wrap the ML.FORECAST call inside a CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE statement so the result is persisted for Looker.
choices.explanation: Persisting forecasts in a table is a standard BI integration pattern.

choices.text: Use ML.PREDICT with a future date table joined by week to generate forecasts directly.
choices.explanation: ML.PREDICT does not support time-series forecasting horizons for ARIMA_PLUS models.

choices.text: Call ML.RECOMMEND with a horizon parameter to produce forward-looking demand values.
choices.explanation: ML.RECOMMEND is for matrix factorization recommender models, not time-series forecasting.

choices.text: Use ML.EVALUATE with a future window to extrapolate predictions beyond the training horizon.
choices.explanation: ML.EVALUATE returns metrics on labeled data and cannot extrapolate forecasts.

questions.tip: Pair the right forecasting function with a persistence pattern.
questions.explanation:
ARIMA_PLUS models in BigQuery ML have a dedicated forecasting function and are commonly persisted into BI-friendly tables.

**Why it works:** ML.FORECAST accepts a horizon and confidence_level inside a STRUCT, and wrapping the result in CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE materializes it for Looker.

**Why the others don't work:**
- ML.PREDICT for time series: not the supported call for ARIMA_PLUS forecasting.
- ML.RECOMMEND: belongs to recommender models, not forecasting.
- ML.EVALUATE: returns evaluation metrics, not forward predictions.

skills: 1.2.1: Building applications by using ML APIs from Model Garden.
questions.question:
The operations team at a logistics company needs to extract printed text from millions of scanned shipment labels stored in Cloud Storage. They want to add an event-driven workflow that processes each new image as it lands and writes the extracted text to BigQuery. The team has limited ML experience and wants to avoid training a custom model.

Which approach provides the MOST suitable solution with the least operational overhead?

choices.text: Trigger a Cloud Functions function on Cloud Storage finalize events that calls the Cloud Vision API `images:annotate` method with the `TEXT_DETECTION` feature and writes results to BigQuery.
choices.explanation: Cloud Vision is a Model Garden ML API providing pre-trained OCR; an event-driven function gives a serverless, low-overhead pipeline.

choices.text: Train a custom Vertex AI AutoML Vision model on a labeled subset of the labels, deploy it to a Vertex AI endpoint, and call it from Cloud Functions for each new file.
choices.explanation: AutoML Vision is for classification or object detection, not generic OCR, and adds training and endpoint cost without benefit.

choices.text: Run a scheduled Dataproc job each hour that reads new images from Cloud Storage and uses an open source Tesseract container to perform OCR before loading BigQuery.
choices.explanation: Tesseract on Dataproc requires cluster management, batches results hourly rather than reactively, and skips Model Garden APIs entirely.

choices.text: Use the Cloud Translation API on each image after uploading the binary content as a translation request, then parse the response to get text.
choices.explanation: Cloud Translation does not accept image inputs or perform OCR; it translates supplied text strings only.

questions.tip: Match the task to the pre-trained Model Garden API designed for it.
questions.explanation:
Cloud Vision exposes a managed OCR endpoint that returns detected text directly. Pairing it with a Cloud Storage trigger gives reactive, serverless processing.

**Why it works:** `TEXT_DETECTION` returns full text annotations from images; Cloud Functions integrates natively with Cloud Storage finalize events.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AutoML Vision: solves classification, not OCR.
- Dataproc + Tesseract: heavy cluster ops and not event-driven.
- Cloud Translation: does not accept images or perform OCR.

skills: 1.2.1: Building applications by using ML APIs from Model Garden.
questions.question:
During a customer experience review, a retail company decides to score the sentiment of free-text product reviews arriving in a Pub/Sub topic. The data science team wants a managed solution with no model training and a simple per-document score and magnitude.

Which Model Garden ML API should the team integrate?

choices.text: Cloud Natural Language API `analyzeSentiment` method, called from a Dataflow streaming pipeline that reads Pub/Sub messages and writes scored rows to BigQuery.
choices.explanation: Natural Language API returns score and magnitude per document with no training required, and Dataflow integrates Pub/Sub to BigQuery cleanly.

choices.text: Speech-to-Text API streaming recognition, with the resulting transcript scored by a custom regex on positive and negative words.
choices.explanation: Speech-to-Text handles audio, not text reviews, and regex scoring is not an ML API.

choices.text: Vertex AI AutoML Tables, trained on review text features and deployed to a batch prediction job each night.
choices.explanation: AutoML Tables is for tabular structured data and requires labeled training, contradicting the no-training requirement.

choices.text: Cloud Translation API in detect-language mode, using the language confidence score as a proxy for sentiment polarity.
choices.explanation: Language detection confidence has no relationship to sentiment polarity.

questions.tip: Pick the pre-trained API whose response shape already matches the desired output.
questions.explanation:
The Natural Language API returns a numeric sentiment score and magnitude directly, satisfying the requirement without any training.

**Why it works:** `analyzeSentiment` is a managed pre-trained endpoint and Dataflow streams Pub/Sub to BigQuery as a built-in template.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Speech-to-Text: wrong modality.
- AutoML Tables: requires training, wrong data type.
- Translation detect-language: does not measure sentiment.

skills: 1.2.1: Building applications by using ML APIs from Model Garden.
questions.question:
The engineering team is evaluating ways to enrich a media archive of mp4 files in Cloud Storage. They want to surface scene-level shot changes and tag recognizable objects using a pre-trained Model Garden ML API rather than building a custom model.

Which TWO actions correctly implement this with the Video Intelligence API?

choices.text: Call `videos:annotate` with the `SHOT_CHANGE_DETECTION` feature, passing the Cloud Storage URI of each video as `inputUri`.
choices.explanation: Shot change detection is a built-in feature returning timestamped shot boundaries directly.

choices.text: Call `videos:annotate` with the `LABEL_DETECTION` feature to receive entity labels with confidence scores at shot, segment, or frame level.
choices.explanation: Label detection returns recognizable objects and concepts with confidence and timing.

choices.text: Train a Vertex AI AutoML Video Object Tracking model on the archive and deploy it to a batch endpoint for each new file.
choices.explanation: Custom training contradicts the requirement to use a pre-trained Model Garden API.

choices.text: Convert each video to individual frames in Cloud Storage and call the Cloud Vision API `LABEL_DETECTION` on every frame.
choices.explanation: This loses temporal context, multiplies cost, and ignores the dedicated Video Intelligence API.

choices.text: Use the Cloud Natural Language API on the file metadata to infer scene and object information from the title.
choices.explanation: Filename text is unrelated to actual visual content and Natural Language analyses text, not video.

questions.tip: Look for the dedicated features the API exposes for video analysis.
questions.explanation:
Video Intelligence exposes purpose-built features for shot detection and label detection that operate directly on videos in Cloud Storage.

**Why it works:** Both `SHOT_CHANGE_DETECTION` and `LABEL_DETECTION` are first-class features of `videos:annotate` and accept a `gs://` URI.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AutoML Video: requires training, not pre-trained.
- Per-frame Vision: wasteful and loses temporal info.
- Natural Language on filename: unrelated to visual content.

skills: 1.2.2: Building applications by using industry-specific APIs, including Document AI API and Retail API.
questions.question:
Following a board decision to digitize accounts payable, a finance department needs to automatically extract supplier name, invoice number, line items, and totals from PDF invoices uploaded to Cloud Storage. They want a managed solution that returns structured fields without training a model from scratch.

Which Document AI processor should the team use?

choices.text: Use the Document AI Invoice parser processor by calling `projects.locations.processors:process` with the PDF as inline content or a Cloud Storage reference.
choices.explanation: The Invoice parser is a specialized pre-trained processor that returns invoice-specific entities such as supplier, line items, and totals.

choices.text: Use the Document AI Form Parser processor and write custom regex on the returned key-value pairs to identify invoice fields.
choices.explanation: Form Parser is generic and returns untyped key-value pairs; it does not natively recognize invoice entities like line items.

choices.text: Use the Document AI Optical Character Recognition processor and parse the raw text in a downstream Cloud Function.
choices.explanation: OCR returns only raw text and layout; downstream parsing reinvents what the Invoice parser already does.

choices.text: Use the Document AI Identity processor configured for invoice schemas.
choices.explanation: The Identity processor is designed for ID documents like passports and licenses, not invoices.

questions.tip: Industry-specific processors return typed entities aligned to their document class.
questions.explanation:
Document AI ships specialized processors for common document types. The Invoice parser is purpose-built and returns the exact entities required.

**Why it works:** Invoice parser outputs typed entities for `supplier_name`, `invoice_id`, `line_item`, `total_amount`, etc., directly from the PDF.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Form Parser: generic key-value, no invoice schema.
- OCR: raw text only, requires custom parsing.
- Identity processor: for IDs, not invoices.

skills: 1.2.2: Building applications by using industry-specific APIs, including Document AI API and Retail API.
questions.question:
An online retailer wants to add a Recommended for You section on its product detail pages, personalized to each shopper based on past behavior. The team has a product catalog and historical user events stored in BigQuery and wants to avoid building a custom recommender.

Which approach is the MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Import the catalog and user events into the Retail API, create a Recommended for You serving config, and call `predict` from the storefront with the user's visitor and product IDs.
choices.explanation: The Retail API provides managed recommendation models for retail with placement-specific serving configs like Recommended for You.

choices.text: Train a Vertex AI custom two-tower model on the BigQuery data and deploy it to an endpoint, calling it from the storefront for each page view.
choices.explanation: This is a high-effort custom path; the Retail API already provides a managed equivalent with retail-tuned models.

choices.text: Use the Cloud Natural Language API to extract entities from product descriptions and recommend the products with the most overlapping entities.
choices.explanation: Entity overlap ignores user behavior and personalization, which is the core requirement.

choices.text: Use BigQuery ML to fit a `KMEANS` model on user events and recommend the top-selling product within each user's cluster.
choices.explanation: Cluster popularity is not personalized at the user-product level and lacks the retail-specific features the Retail API uses.

questions.tip: Industry APIs encapsulate the model, the serving placement, and the data schema for that vertical.
questions.explanation:
The Retail API is Google's managed personalization service for ecommerce, with named placements such as Recommended for You that map to tuned models.

**Why it works:** It accepts the catalog and user events, trains and serves models for retail-specific placements, and exposes a `predict` endpoint per visitor.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Custom Vertex AI two-tower: high effort, duplicates the managed offering.
- Natural Language entity overlap: not personalized.
- BigQuery ML clustering: coarse and not user-personalized.

skills: 1.2.2: Building applications by using industry-specific APIs, including Document AI API and Retail API.
questions.question:
The data engineering team is preparing to onboard a retailer onto the Retail API for search and recommendations. They need to make the product catalog and shopper behavior available so that managed models can be trained.

Which TWO actions are required to ingest data into the Retail API?

choices.text: Import the product catalog using `products:import` from a BigQuery table or Cloud Storage JSON Lines file that conforms to the Product schema.
choices.explanation: Catalog import accepts BigQuery or GCS sources following the Product proto schema.

choices.text: Import historical user events using `userEvents:import` with event types such as `detail-page-view`, `add-to-cart`, and `purchase-complete`.
choices.explanation: User events are required for personalization quality and are imported via the dedicated method.

choices.text: Train a custom Vertex AI Pipelines workflow that writes embeddings to a Vertex AI Vector Search index before calling Retail API predict.
choices.explanation: Retail API manages its own embeddings; an external vector index is not part of ingestion.

choices.text: Upload audio recordings of customer service calls so the Retail API can derive intent signals.
choices.explanation: Retail API does not consume audio recordings as a behavioral signal.

choices.text: Configure a Cloud Translation API glossary so product titles are normalized before ingest.
choices.explanation: A translation glossary is unrelated to catalog ingestion requirements.

questions.tip: Think about the two data domains the Retail API needs: what is for sale and how shoppers behave.
questions.explanation:
The Retail API requires two foundational imports: the catalog of products and the historical user events that describe shopper behavior.

**Why it works:** `products:import` and `userEvents:import` accept BigQuery or GCS sources and feed managed model training and serving.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Vector Search index: not part of Retail API ingestion.
- Audio recordings: unsupported input.
- Translation glossary: unrelated.

skills: 1.2.2: Building applications by using industry-specific APIs, including Document AI API and Retail API.
questions.question: Arrange the steps to set up an automated invoice extraction pipeline using Document AI in the correct order.

choices.text: Enable the Document AI API in the Google Cloud project.
choices.explanation: The API must be enabled before any processor can be created or invoked.

choices.text: Create an Invoice parser processor in the desired region and note its processor ID.
choices.explanation: A processor instance with a stable ID is required to send documents to.

choices.text: Send PDF invoices from Cloud Storage to the processor using the process method.
choices.explanation: With the processor ready, documents can be processed individually or in batch.

choices.text: Persist the returned typed entities to BigQuery for downstream analytics.
choices.explanation: Storing the structured output enables reporting and integration with finance systems.

questions.tip: Provisioning comes before invocation, and invocation comes before storage of results.
questions.explanation: Document AI requires enabling the API, creating a processor instance, then submitting documents and finally persisting the structured output for downstream use.

skills: 1.2.3: Implementing retrieval augmented generation (RAG) applications by using Vertex AI Agent Builder.
questions.question:
The knowledge management team at a law firm wants an internal assistant that answers staff questions using only the firm's own policy PDFs and contracts in Cloud Storage. They want grounded answers with citations and minimal infrastructure to manage.

Which approach BEST implements this with Vertex AI Agent Builder?

choices.text: Create a Vertex AI Search data store pointing at the Cloud Storage bucket of unstructured documents, attach it to a search app, and enable summarization with citations.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI Search ingests unstructured Cloud Storage data and provides grounded summarization with citations as a managed RAG pattern in Agent Builder.

choices.text: Fine-tune a Gemini model on the policy PDFs using Vertex AI supervised tuning and serve it from a private endpoint.
choices.explanation: Fine-tuning bakes facts into weights without citations and is far higher effort than retrieval grounding for document Q and A.

choices.text: Concatenate every PDF into a single text file and include it as a system prompt for each call to the Gemini API.
choices.explanation: This will exceed context limits, increases token cost on every call, and provides no citations or freshness controls.

choices.text: Build a custom solution using Cloud Functions to do regex search across the PDFs and return matching paragraphs to the user.
choices.explanation: Regex search misses semantic meaning and reinvents the retrieval and grounding that Agent Builder provides natively.

questions.tip: Agent Builder provides managed retrieval and grounding for unstructured corpora.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Search inside Agent Builder is the managed RAG service: it indexes unstructured content from Cloud Storage and serves grounded summaries with citations.

**Why it works:** A data store on a Cloud Storage bucket plus a search app produces a citation-aware answer experience without custom retrieval code.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Fine-tuning: no citations and high effort.
- Mega prompt: exceeds context, expensive, ungrounded.
- Regex Cloud Function: not semantic, no grounding.

skills: 1.2.3: Implementing retrieval augmented generation (RAG) applications by using Vertex AI Agent Builder.
questions.question:
After reviewing quarterly spending, an enterprise wants to ensure that responses generated by its Vertex AI Agent Builder assistant are grounded in the company's own data store and that hallucinations are minimized when the corpus does not contain the answer.

Which configuration provides the MOST appropriate safeguard?

choices.text: Enable grounding on the Gemini-powered agent so that generated responses are constrained to retrieved snippets, and configure a fallback message when no relevant chunks are returned above the grounding threshold.
choices.explanation: Grounding restricts generation to retrieved evidence and the threshold or check-grounding response handles low-confidence cases.

choices.text: Increase the model temperature to 1.5 so the model can express uncertainty when the corpus does not contain the answer.
choices.explanation: Higher temperature increases randomness and hallucination, not factual safety.

choices.text: Disable retrieval and rely on the base Gemini model's general world knowledge to answer enterprise questions.
choices.explanation: This removes grounding entirely and is the opposite of what is required.

choices.text: Reduce the number of retrieved chunks to one, ensuring only the highest-ranked passage is used regardless of relevance.
choices.explanation: Forcing a single chunk does not protect against irrelevant retrieval and reduces answer quality.

questions.tip: RAG safety relies on grounding the answer in retrieved context and handling low-confidence retrieval explicitly.
questions.explanation:
Grounding constrains the generative answer to retrieved passages from the data store; combining it with a confidence threshold handles questions outside the corpus gracefully.

**Why it works:** Agent Builder grounds Gemini on retrieved chunks from Vertex AI Search and exposes confidence signals to support fallback.

**Why the others don't work:**
- High temperature: increases hallucination.
- No retrieval: ungrounded answers.
- Single chunk: still ungrounded if irrelevant.

skills: 1.2.3: Implementing retrieval augmented generation (RAG) applications by using Vertex AI Agent Builder.
questions.question:
You are designing a RAG assistant in Vertex AI Agent Builder that needs to answer questions over both a folder of PDF product manuals in Cloud Storage and a structured BigQuery table of frequently asked questions.

Which TWO actions correctly configure the data sources?

choices.text: Create an unstructured data store in Vertex AI Search that points to the Cloud Storage URI prefix containing the PDF manuals.
choices.explanation: Unstructured data stores accept Cloud Storage prefixes and index documents for semantic retrieval.

choices.text: Create a structured data store in Vertex AI Search backed by the BigQuery FAQ table, mapping the question and answer columns in the schema.
choices.explanation: Structured data stores ingest BigQuery tables and expose row fields for retrieval and grounding.

choices.text: Export the BigQuery FAQ rows as plain text files into the same Cloud Storage prefix as the PDFs to simplify ingestion.
choices.explanation: Mixing structured and unstructured into one bucket loses field semantics and is unnecessary when a structured data store is supported.

choices.text: Embed every PDF and BigQuery row manually using a Sentence Transformers container on Compute Engine and store vectors in Memorystore for Redis.
choices.explanation: Agent Builder manages embeddings and indexing; this rebuilds infrastructure that already exists.

choices.text: Set up a Cloud Composer DAG that copies the PDFs into BigQuery as base64 strings before indexing.
choices.explanation: Storing PDFs as base64 in BigQuery defeats the unstructured indexing path and adds unnecessary complexity.

questions.tip: Match each source's nature to the corresponding data store type.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Search distinguishes unstructured and structured data stores, enabling each source to be indexed with the right schema.

**Why it works:** Cloud Storage maps cleanly to unstructured; BigQuery maps cleanly to structured with schema mapping.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Flatten BigQuery to GCS: loses field semantics.
- Custom embeddings on Compute Engine: duplicates managed indexing.
- Composer base64 ingest: adds complexity for no benefit.

skills: 1.2.3: Implementing retrieval augmented generation (RAG) applications by using Vertex AI Agent Builder.
questions.question: Arrange the steps to build a RAG-powered search app in Vertex AI Agent Builder in the correct order.

choices.text: Create a Vertex AI Search data store referencing the source corpus in Cloud Storage or BigQuery.
choices.explanation: The data store defines the retrieval corpus and must exist before an app can use it.

choices.text: Create a search or chat app and attach the data store to it.
choices.explanation: The app provides the serving surface and binds to one or more data stores.

choices.text: Enable summarization with grounding so generated responses cite retrieved passages.
choices.explanation: Grounded summarization layers a generative answer on top of retrieved results.

choices.text: Integrate the app's API into the client application and monitor query metrics.
choices.explanation: Integration and observability close the loop on the deployed RAG experience.

questions.tip: Build the corpus first, then the app surface, then enable generation, then integrate.
questions.explanation: Agent Builder follows a layered model: data store, then app, then generative grounding, then integration with the client and monitoring.

skills: 1.3.1: Preparing data for AutoML, including feature selection, data labeling, and Tabular Workflows on AutoML.
questions.question:
The operations team at a logistics startup has 80,000 unlabeled photos of warehouse incidents and wants to train an AutoML image classification model in Vertex AI. Internal staff lack the bandwidth to label the dataset themselves, and leadership has approved a managed workflow that uses Google-supplied human labelers following a written labeling guide.

Which approach should the team use to obtain labeled training data?

choices.text: Create a Vertex AI data labeling job, upload the unlabeled images to a Vertex AI managed dataset, attach a labeling instruction PDF, and request human labelers from Google
choices.explanation: Vertex AI data labeling jobs use Google-managed labelers guided by an uploaded instructions document.

choices.text: Run AutoML training directly on the unlabeled images and rely on AutoML's self-supervised pretraining to infer categories
choices.explanation: AutoML image classification requires labeled examples; it does not auto-label arbitrary unlabeled photos.

choices.text: Use the Vision API to generate object localization annotations and import the JSON output as training labels without human review
choices.explanation: Vision API labels are generic and will not match the project's specific incident taxonomy.

choices.text: Configure a Dataflow pipeline that hashes each image filename to one of the candidate label classes and imports the result into the Vertex AI dataset
choices.explanation: Hashing produces random labels and would yield a model that performs no better than chance.

questions.tip: Identify the managed Vertex AI feature designed for human-in-the-loop labeling.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI data labeling jobs are the managed workflow for obtaining human labels on images, text, or video, where Google provides the labeler workforce and the customer supplies an instruction document.

**Why it works:** The data labeling job ties the unlabeled dataset, the labeling guide, and the human workforce together, returning a labeled Vertex AI managed dataset ready for AutoML.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Self-supervised AutoML: AutoML image classification needs labels.
- Vision API auto-labels: generic categories, not the custom incident taxonomy.
- Hash-based pipeline: assigns labels at random, producing useless training data.

skills: 1.3.1: Preparing data for AutoML, including feature selection, data labeling, and Tabular Workflows on AutoML.
questions.question:
A data science team at an insurance company is preparing a 90-million-row claims table in BigQuery for an AutoML tabular classification model. They want a managed pipeline that exposes individual feature engineering, architecture search, and training steps as configurable Vertex AI Pipelines components, so that they can later swap the architecture search algorithm without rewriting the rest of the workflow.

Which approach BEST satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: Run the Tabular Workflow for End-to-End AutoML on Vertex AI Pipelines, pointing the BigQuery source at the claims table and customizing the prebuilt pipeline components as needed
choices.explanation: Tabular Workflows expose AutoML as a Vertex AI Pipelines DAG with replaceable components for feature engineering, architecture search, and training.

choices.text: Train a classic AutoML tabular model from the Vertex AI console and rely on its hidden defaults for feature engineering and architecture search
choices.explanation: The classic AutoML tabular flow runs as an opaque managed job and does not expose pipeline components for customization.

choices.text: Export the BigQuery table to CSV in Cloud Storage and submit a Vertex AI custom training job that calls a hand-written XGBoost script
choices.explanation: Custom training abandons AutoML entirely and requires the team to author all feature engineering and search logic.

choices.text: Use BigQuery ML AUTOML_CLASSIFIER and rely on scheduled queries to retrain the model when the claims table updates
choices.explanation: BigQuery ML AutoML runs inside BigQuery and does not expose Vertex AI Pipelines components.

questions.tip: Look for the AutoML offering that exposes its internals as Vertex AI Pipelines components.
questions.explanation:
Tabular Workflows on Vertex AI run AutoML as a Vertex AI Pipelines DAG whose components, including feature transformations and architecture search, can be swapped or tuned individually.

**Why it works:** The team gets AutoML quality plus the ability to override individual pipeline steps without re-implementing the entire workflow.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Classic AutoML tabular: hides its internal steps and offers no per-component customization.
- Custom training script: removes the AutoML benefit the team wants.
- BigQuery ML AutoML: runs inside BigQuery, not as a Vertex AI Pipelines DAG.

skills: 1.3.1: Preparing data for AutoML, including feature selection, data labeling, and Tabular Workflows on AutoML.
questions.question:
You are preparing a 12-million-row customer churn dataset in BigQuery for an AutoML tabular classification model in Vertex AI. The target column has roughly 4 percent positive examples, and the table contains a raw timestamp column, several free-text comment fields, and a customer_id column that uniquely identifies every row.

Which TWO data preparation actions improve AutoML training quality for this scenario?

choices.text: Exclude the customer_id column from the feature set, since unique identifiers cannot generalize and add no predictive signal
choices.explanation: Per-row unique identifiers cause overfitting and Google's tabular guidance recommends excluding them.

choices.text: Mark the raw timestamp column as a Timestamp data type so AutoML can derive cyclical and trend features automatically
choices.explanation: Declaring the column as Timestamp lets AutoML extract day-of-week, month, and other temporal features.

choices.text: Manually one-hot encode every categorical column to dozens of binary columns before importing the table
choices.explanation: AutoML tabular handles categorical encoding internally; pre-encoding only inflates the schema.

choices.text: Drop the minority class rows so the dataset is perfectly balanced 50/50 before training
choices.explanation: Discarding positives throws away signal; AutoML supports class weighting or stratified split instead.

choices.text: Concatenate all free-text comment fields into the customer_id column to give AutoML more context per row
choices.explanation: This corrupts the identifier and mixes incompatible semantic types in one column.

questions.tip: Think about what AutoML expects to derive automatically and what only adds noise.
questions.explanation:
AutoML tabular benefits when truly identifying columns are excluded and when columns are typed correctly so the service can derive richer features.

**Why it works:** Removing customer_id prevents memorization, and typing the timestamp lets AutoML auto-extract calendar features.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Manual one-hot encoding: redundant with built-in transformations.
- Dropping minority rows: discards rare-class signal.
- Merging text into customer_id: destroys both columns.

skills: 1.3.1: Preparing data for AutoML, including feature selection, data labeling, and Tabular Workflows on AutoML.
questions.question:
Arrange the following steps in the correct order for preparing a labeled image dataset for AutoML image classification in Vertex AI when starting from raw, unlabeled images.

Put the steps in the order they should be performed.

choices.text: Upload the raw images to a Cloud Storage bucket in the same region as the Vertex AI dataset
choices.explanation: Source images must live in regional Cloud Storage before they can be referenced.

choices.text: Create a Vertex AI managed image dataset and import the images from the Cloud Storage URIs
choices.explanation: The managed dataset registers the images with Vertex AI for downstream tooling.

choices.text: Submit a Vertex AI data labeling job, attaching the labeling instruction document and selecting the label classes
choices.explanation: Labeling jobs operate on an existing managed dataset.

choices.text: Train an AutoML image classification model on the now-labeled managed dataset
choices.explanation: Training is the final step once labels are populated.

questions.tip: Trace the dependencies: data must exist, then be registered, then be labeled, then be used.
questions.explanation: AutoML image training requires a labeled managed dataset, which in turn requires images registered into Vertex AI from Cloud Storage, which itself requires the bytes to be uploaded first.

skills: 1.3.2: Using available data types, including tabular, text, speech, images, and videos, to train custom models.
questions.question:
The marketing analytics group at a media company wants to classify uploaded promotional clips into five content categories. They have 6,000 short MP4 files already labeled with one category each, and they want to train without writing model code. The team plans to evaluate AutoML before deciding whether to invest in a custom training pipeline.

Which AutoML offering should they use to build the initial model?

choices.text: AutoML Video classification on a Vertex AI managed video dataset, importing the labeled MP4 references from Cloud Storage
choices.explanation: AutoML Video classification trains a single-label or multi-label clip classifier from labeled video files.

choices.text: AutoML Image classification, sampling one frame per video and treating the problem as still-image classification
choices.explanation: Single-frame sampling discards temporal signal and is not the AutoML recommendation for video classification.

choices.text: AutoML Text classification on transcripts produced by the Speech-to-Text API for each clip
choices.explanation: Text-only classification ignores the visual content the team wants to categorize.

choices.text: AutoML Tabular classification on a feature table containing video duration, codec, and bitrate
choices.explanation: These metadata columns do not encode the content of the clip, only its container properties.

questions.tip: Pick the AutoML data modality that matches the raw input the team holds.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI offers dedicated AutoML solutions per data type, and AutoML Video classification is purpose-built for whole-clip categorization tasks like this one.

**Why it works:** The labeled MP4 corpus maps directly onto a managed video dataset, and AutoML Video produces a clip classifier without custom code.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Image AutoML on a single frame: loses temporal information.
- Text AutoML on transcripts: ignores visuals.
- Tabular AutoML on container metadata: those columns are not predictive of content.

skills: 1.3.2: Using available data types, including tabular, text, speech, images, and videos, to train custom models.
questions.question:
During a customer-support modernization project, the engineering team wants to train an AutoML text classification model in Vertex AI on roughly 200,000 historical support emails labeled with one of seven product areas. Each email is currently a single row in a BigQuery table along with its label. They want the simplest path to producing a managed text dataset for AutoML.

Which approach is the MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Export the BigQuery table to a JSONL file in Cloud Storage following the AutoML text import schema, then create a Vertex AI text dataset and import from that JSONL
choices.explanation: AutoML text uses JSONL import files referencing inline content or text URIs, and exporting from BigQuery is straightforward.

choices.text: Render each email as a 1024x1024 image of the rendered text and import them into a Vertex AI image dataset
choices.explanation: Converting text to images discards token-level signal and uses the wrong AutoML modality.

choices.text: Stream each row to Pub/Sub and use Dataflow to write protobuf shards that AutoML text reads natively
choices.explanation: AutoML text does not consume protobuf streams; the documented format is JSONL.

choices.text: Train an AutoML tabular model directly on the BigQuery table, using the email body column as a tabular feature
choices.explanation: AutoML tabular treats long free text as a generic string feature and is not the documented modality for text classification.

questions.tip: Use the data modality and import format that the AutoML offering documents.
questions.explanation:
AutoML text classification expects a Vertex AI text dataset populated from a JSONL import file in Cloud Storage following the documented schema.

**Why it works:** BigQuery can export the labeled rows to JSONL directly, matching the AutoML text import contract.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Rendering text to images: wrong modality.
- Pub/Sub plus protobuf: not a supported AutoML import path.
- AutoML tabular on email bodies: tabular treats long text generically and is not the recommended fit.

skills: 1.3.2: Using available data types, including tabular, text, speech, images, and videos, to train custom models.
questions.question:
A platform team is documenting which AutoML data types are first-class citizens in Vertex AI managed datasets so that solution architects can quickly choose the right modality. They want to publish an internal cheat sheet that lists only the AutoML offerings supported by Vertex AI today.

Which TWO of the following are valid AutoML modalities offered through Vertex AI managed datasets?

choices.text: AutoML Image classification and object detection on managed image datasets
choices.explanation: Vertex AI offers AutoML Image classification and object detection on image datasets.

choices.text: AutoML Text classification, entity extraction, and sentiment analysis on managed text datasets
choices.explanation: Vertex AI Text AutoML supports classification, entity extraction, and sentiment analysis.

choices.text: AutoML Audio speaker-diarization training on managed speech datasets
choices.explanation: Vertex AI does not offer a dedicated AutoML speaker-diarization training service; speaker diarization is a Speech-to-Text API feature.

choices.text: AutoML Time-series anomaly detection on managed point-cloud datasets
choices.explanation: There is no AutoML point-cloud dataset type, and time-series anomaly detection is not an AutoML modality.

choices.text: AutoML 3D mesh generation on managed CAD datasets
choices.explanation: Vertex AI does not offer 3D mesh generation as an AutoML offering.

questions.tip: Match each option to a documented AutoML data type in Vertex AI.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI's AutoML offerings cover tabular, text, image, and video modalities through managed datasets, with text supporting classification, entity extraction, and sentiment, and image supporting classification and object detection.

**Why it works:** Both selected statements describe documented AutoML offerings on real managed dataset types.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Diarization training: belongs to Speech-to-Text, not AutoML training.
- Point-cloud anomaly detection: not an AutoML data type.
- 3D mesh generation: not offered by AutoML.

skills: 1.3.2: Using available data types, including tabular, text, speech, images, and videos, to train custom models.
questions.question: Match each business problem to the AutoML data type that BEST fits training a custom model in Vertex AI.

slots.label: Categorize uploaded product photos into one of 200 catalog categories

Classify uploaded support tickets into seven product areas
Detect when a person enters the frame in security camera footage

choices.text: AutoML Tabular

choices.text: AutoML Text

choices.text: AutoML Video

questions.tip: Match the raw input modality to the AutoML data type designed for it.
questions.explanation: Each AutoML modality is designed around a specific input data type, so the correct mapping follows directly from the raw input the team holds.

skills: 1.3.3: Using AutoML for tabular data.
questions.question:
Following a board decision to launch a new credit risk product, the analytics team wants to train an AutoML tabular binary classification model in Vertex AI on a 30-million-row applications table in BigQuery. They want AutoML to optimize specifically for the area under the precision-recall curve because the positive class (default) is rare and ranking quality matters more than overall accuracy.

Which configuration should they choose when creating the training job?

choices.text: Set the optimization objective to maximize-au-prc when launching the AutoML tabular classification training job
choices.explanation: AutoML tabular classification supports maximize-au-prc as a training optimization objective for imbalanced ranking problems.

choices.text: Train with the default optimization objective and rely on a post-training threshold sweep to recover precision-recall performance
choices.explanation: Threshold tuning cannot change which metric the trainer optimized; the wrong objective leaves quality on the table.

choices.text: Choose AutoML tabular regression and set the loss to mean squared error on the binary label
choices.explanation: Treating a binary label as regression produces a continuous score but discards the documented classification optimization objectives.

choices.text: Use AutoML forecasting with a horizon of one and the binary label as the target column
choices.explanation: Forecasting is for time-indexed targets, not for static binary classification.

questions.tip: Look at the documented AutoML tabular optimization objectives for binary classification.
questions.explanation:
AutoML tabular classification exposes per-job optimization objectives, including maximize-au-prc for binary problems where ranking the rare positive class well is the priority.

**Why it works:** Selecting maximize-au-prc tells AutoML to optimize directly for area under the precision-recall curve during training.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Default objective plus threshold sweep: cannot retroactively change the trained metric.
- Regression on a binary label: bypasses AutoML's classification objectives.
- Forecasting on a binary label: wrong AutoML offering for static prediction.

skills: 1.3.3: Using AutoML for tabular data.
questions.question:
To reduce infrastructure costs, the data team is running an AutoML tabular regression experiment in Vertex AI on a 4-million-row training table. They want to cap training spend by limiting how many node-hours AutoML may use, and they accept that early stopping may shorten the run if no further improvement is detected.

Which training configuration MOST directly enforces this cost cap?

choices.text: Set the training budget in node-hours when launching the AutoML tabular training job and leave early stopping enabled
choices.explanation: AutoML tabular training accepts a node-hours budget and enables early stopping by default.

choices.text: Configure a billing budget alert at the project level for the expected dollar amount
choices.explanation: Budget alerts notify but do not stop the training job; they do not enforce a node-hour cap.

choices.text: Set the Vertex AI Pipelines DAG timeout to two hours and rely on the orchestrator to cancel the job
choices.explanation: A pipeline timeout aborts mid-training and wastes the partial run rather than letting AutoML finish gracefully under a budget.

choices.text: Reduce the BigQuery table to 100,000 rows so that AutoML naturally finishes training in less time
choices.explanation: Down-sampling changes the training data and is not the documented mechanism for capping AutoML cost.

questions.tip: Find the AutoML training parameter purpose-built for spend control.
questions.explanation:
AutoML tabular jobs accept a training budget expressed in milli node-hours, and early stopping ends the run if additional budget would not improve the model.

**Why it works:** The node-hour budget is the documented hard cap on training cost.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Billing alerts: notify but do not stop training.
- Pipeline timeout: aborts the run rather than honoring a graceful budget.
- Down-sampling: alters the dataset rather than capping spend.

skills: 1.3.3: Using AutoML for tabular data.
questions.question:
After reviewing quarterly spending, the engineering team has trained an AutoML tabular classification model in Vertex AI and now needs to score 50 million rows that arrive once a day from BigQuery. Latency per request is not a concern because the consumers read the daily output as a batch.

Which TWO actions correctly produce predictions for this workload using documented AutoML tabular options?

choices.text: Submit a Vertex AI batch prediction job that reads the input table directly from BigQuery and writes results to a destination BigQuery table
choices.explanation: AutoML tabular models support BigQuery as a batch prediction input and output.

choices.text: Submit a batch prediction job that reads JSONL inputs from Cloud Storage and writes JSONL outputs back to Cloud Storage
choices.explanation: Cloud Storage JSONL is also a documented batch prediction input and output format.

choices.text: Stream every row through Pub/Sub to a Vertex AI online endpoint at 10,000 QPS to obtain predictions
choices.explanation: Online endpoints serve low-latency requests and are unnecessarily expensive for daily batch scoring.

choices.text: Export the AutoML model weights to a TensorFlow.js bundle and run scoring inside a Cloud Run container
choices.explanation: AutoML tabular models cannot be exported as runnable artifacts in this manner.

choices.text: Schedule the BigQuery ML ML.PREDICT function against the AutoML tabular model that lives in Vertex AI
choices.explanation: ML.PREDICT works on BigQuery ML models, not on Vertex AI AutoML tabular models hosted in Vertex AI.

questions.tip: Identify the documented input and output formats for AutoML tabular batch prediction.
questions.explanation:
AutoML tabular batch prediction supports BigQuery and Cloud Storage JSONL as both input source and output destination, which is the right tool for daily, latency-tolerant scoring.

**Why it works:** Both options match the documented batch prediction contract for AutoML tabular models.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Online endpoint at 10,000 QPS: overkill and expensive for batch.
- Exporting AutoML weights to TensorFlow.js: not supported.
- ML.PREDICT on a Vertex AI AutoML model: ML.PREDICT targets BigQuery ML models.
