skills: 1.3.4: Creating forecasting models by using AutoML.
questions.question:
The supply chain team at a grocery chain wants to forecast next-day sales for each of 4,800 store-and-product combinations using three years of daily history stored in BigQuery. Each row contains store_id, product_id, sale_date, units_sold, and several promotion flags. They want a single AutoML forecasting model that learns across all series rather than one model per combination.

Which Vertex AI configuration MOST directly satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: Train an AutoML forecasting model with sale_date as the time column, units_sold as the target, and the concatenation of store_id and product_id as the time series identifier column
choices.explanation: AutoML forecasting trains one model across many series when given a time series identifier column.

choices.text: Loop over each store-and-product pair and submit a separate AutoML tabular regression job for each one
choices.explanation: AutoML tabular regression is not the forecasting offering, and one model per pair contradicts the team's stated requirement.

choices.text: Train an AutoML classification model with units_sold bucketed into 10 categories and store_id and product_id as features
choices.explanation: Bucketing a continuous quantity into classes loses precision and is not the forecasting modality.

choices.text: Use AutoML Image classification on plotted sales charts to predict next-day demand from chart shape
choices.explanation: Plotting series as images discards numerical structure and is not a documented forecasting approach.

questions.tip: Look for the AutoML forecasting column that distinguishes individual time series.
questions.explanation:
AutoML forecasting is built around the concept of a time series identifier column that lets a single model train across thousands of related series, conditioned on the identifier and supplied covariates.

**Why it works:** Marking the combined store-and-product key as the time series identifier instructs AutoML to share parameters across series while still distinguishing them.

**Why the others don't work:**
- One model per pair: contradicts the single-model requirement.
- Classification on bucketed sales: wrong modality.
- Image classification on chart screenshots: not a forecasting approach.

skills: 1.3.4: Creating forecasting models by using AutoML.
questions.question:
You are configuring an AutoML forecasting model in Vertex AI to predict daily revenue for the next 14 days. The training table contains a campaign_active boolean column whose values are known in advance for both historical dates and the upcoming 14-day horizon, because marketing schedules are locked.

How should you declare the campaign_active column when configuring the forecasting job?

choices.text: Mark campaign_active as a covariate available at forecast time so AutoML can use its known future values during prediction
choices.explanation: AutoML forecasting distinguishes covariates known at forecast time from those that are not, and uses the known-at-forecast-time values directly.

choices.text: Mark campaign_active as a covariate not available at forecast time so AutoML imputes its future values from history
choices.explanation: Imputing values that are already known wastes information; the column is known in advance.

choices.text: Exclude campaign_active entirely so AutoML cannot leak future-period information into training
choices.explanation: Known-future covariates are not leakage; they are a documented forecasting input type.

choices.text: Set campaign_active as the time column to align historical and future records
choices.explanation: The time column must be a date or timestamp, not a boolean flag.

questions.tip: Match the column behavior to the AutoML forecasting covariate types.
questions.explanation:
AutoML forecasting separates covariates into those whose values are known at forecast time, such as planned promotions or holidays, and those that are not. Marketing schedules locked through the horizon belong to the former.

**Why it works:** Declaring it as a covariate available at forecast time supplies real future values to the model.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Not available at forecast time: forces imputation despite real values being known.
- Excluding the column: discards a useful predictor.
- Using it as the time column: only date or timestamp columns are valid.

skills: 1.3.4: Creating forecasting models by using AutoML.
questions.question:
Management has decided that a new AutoML forecasting model in Vertex AI must predict next-week unit sales while accounting for both pre-scheduled holidays and a long-term upward trend in unrelated macroeconomic indicators that are only known historically.

Which TWO column configurations correctly support this design?

choices.text: Configure the holiday calendar columns as covariates available at forecast time
choices.explanation: Holidays are known for the future horizon, so they belong in the at-forecast-time covariate group.

choices.text: Configure the macroeconomic indicator columns as covariates not available at forecast time
choices.explanation: Indicators known only historically belong in the not-at-forecast-time covariate group.

choices.text: Configure unit_sales itself as a covariate available at forecast time so AutoML reuses its labels
choices.explanation: The target column is the variable being predicted; treating it as a known-future covariate would leak labels.

choices.text: Drop the time series identifier column so AutoML treats every row as part of one universal series
choices.explanation: Dropping the identifier conflates distinct series and harms forecast quality.

choices.text: Replace the timestamp column with a row index so AutoML can ignore calendar effects
choices.explanation: AutoML forecasting requires a real time column to learn temporal structure.

questions.tip: Sort each predictor by whether its future values are actually known at prediction time.
questions.explanation:
AutoML forecasting needs predictors classified by whether their future values are known. Holidays are known; macroeconomic indicators in this scenario are not.

**Why it works:** Both selected configurations align each column with its real availability at forecast time.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Treating the target as a known-future covariate: label leakage.
- Dropping the time series identifier: collapses distinct series.
- Replacing the timestamp with a row index: removes the time structure AutoML needs.

skills: 1.3.4: Creating forecasting models by using AutoML.
questions.question: Arrange the following steps for building a Vertex AI AutoML forecasting model from a BigQuery time-series table in the correct order.

choices.text: Create a Vertex AI tabular dataset that points at the BigQuery time-series table
choices.explanation: The managed dataset is the foundation for all subsequent AutoML steps.

choices.text: Specify the time column, target column, time series identifier column, and forecast horizon
choices.explanation: These parameters define the forecasting problem before training.

choices.text: Train the AutoML forecasting model with a chosen training budget
choices.explanation: Training cannot start until the schema and forecast configuration are set.

choices.text: Submit a batch prediction job that produces forecasts for the next horizon window
choices.explanation: Batch prediction is the consumption step after a model is trained.

questions.tip: Each step depends on the previous one; trace the data and configuration flow.
questions.explanation: AutoML forecasting workflows always proceed from registering data, through configuring the forecast schema, to training, and finally to producing forecasts.

skills: 1.3.5: Configuring and debugging trained AutoML models.
questions.question:
During a model review, the engineering team observes that a recently trained AutoML tabular classification model in Vertex AI achieves 99.6 percent accuracy on its training set but only 71 percent accuracy on the held-out test split provided by AutoML. They suspect overfitting and want to confirm by inspecting model evaluation artifacts before retraining.

Which Vertex AI artifact should they examine FIRST to confirm the gap?

choices.text: The model evaluation page in Vertex AI, which reports per-split metrics including the test split confusion matrix and aggregate accuracy
choices.explanation: AutoML's model evaluation surface reports holdout metrics that directly reveal generalization gaps.

choices.text: The Cloud Logging entries for the training job's worker pool, filtered to lines emitted by the trainer container
choices.explanation: Training logs describe job execution, not the test-set quality gap.

choices.text: The IAM audit log entries for the model's resource, filtered to dataset-read events
choices.explanation: Audit logs capture access events, not model accuracy.

choices.text: The Cloud Monitoring dashboard for online prediction request latency on the model's endpoint
choices.explanation: Latency metrics describe serving performance, not training versus test accuracy.

questions.tip: Look for the documented surface that exposes per-split AutoML metrics.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI's model evaluation page is the canonical place to compare training and test split quality on an AutoML tabular model.

**Why it works:** It surfaces aggregate metrics, the confusion matrix, and other split-level diagnostics in one view.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cloud Logging: shows job execution, not metric quality.
- IAM audit logs: capture access, not accuracy.
- Latency dashboards: describe serving, not training-test gap.

skills: 1.3.5: Configuring and debugging trained AutoML models.
questions.question:
After reviewing quarterly spending, an analytics team finds that an AutoML tabular regression model in Vertex AI heavily under-predicts revenue in one geographic region. They want to inspect which features drove a specific surprising prediction so they can debug whether a categorical column is being misinterpreted by the model.

Which Vertex AI capability is the MOST appropriate diagnostic?

choices.text: Enable Vertex Explainable AI feature attributions on the AutoML tabular model and request local explanations for the suspect predictions
choices.explanation: Vertex Explainable AI returns per-prediction feature attributions for AutoML tabular models.

choices.text: Run the BigQuery EXPLAIN statement against the AutoML model to retrieve the SQL query plan
choices.explanation: EXPLAIN returns query plans, not feature attributions for AutoML models.

choices.text: Increase the training budget by 50 percent and retrain, expecting that more compute will reveal the issue
choices.explanation: More compute does not produce per-prediction explanations.

choices.text: Open Cloud Logging and filter prediction requests by user agent to see which client generated the suspect rows
choices.explanation: User agent filtering identifies callers, not feature contributions.

questions.tip: Identify the Vertex AI feature designed for per-prediction feature attributions.
questions.explanation:
Vertex Explainable AI is the documented mechanism for inspecting which input features drove a particular AutoML tabular prediction.

**Why it works:** Local explanations attribute the prediction back to the input features, making categorical-handling bugs visible.

**Why the others don't work:**
- BigQuery EXPLAIN: SQL query plans, unrelated.
- More compute: does not provide attributions.
- User agent filtering: identifies callers, not model behavior.

skills: 1.3.5: Configuring and debugging trained AutoML models.
questions.question:
The engineering team is evaluating an AutoML tabular classification model in Vertex AI that scored well on its test split but performs poorly in production. They suspect that the train, validation, and test split was not representative of production traffic, especially because the dataset spans three years of customer behavior.

Which TWO actions are valid configuration options to address this when retraining?

choices.text: Configure a manual data split using a column whose values flag rows as TRAIN, VALIDATION, or TEST
choices.explanation: AutoML tabular accepts a manual split column, letting the team align splits with business meaning.

choices.text: Configure a chronological data split based on the order date column so the test set contains the most recent rows
choices.explanation: AutoML tabular supports chronological splits, mirroring how the model will face newer data in production.

choices.text: Disable the validation split entirely so all data is used for training and testing simultaneously
choices.explanation: Removing validation prevents AutoML from selecting models, and reusing data for training and testing inflates metrics.

choices.text: Use Cloud Storage object lifecycle rules to delete training rows older than 30 days during the job
choices.explanation: Lifecycle rules act on Cloud Storage objects and do not change AutoML splits.

choices.text: Switch the optimization objective to maximize log loss to compensate for biased splits
choices.explanation: Changing the optimization objective does not address an unrepresentative split.

questions.tip: Recall the documented split strategies that AutoML tabular accepts.
questions.explanation:
AutoML tabular supports manual splits via a flag column and chronological splits via a time column, both of which can produce more realistic test sets when production data drifts over time.

**Why it works:** Either option lets the team match the split to the real generative process behind production traffic.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disabling validation: harms model selection and inflates metrics.
- Lifecycle deletes: out-of-scope mechanism.
- Changing the objective: does not fix split representativeness.

skills: 1.3.5: Configuring and debugging trained AutoML models.
questions.question: Match each observed AutoML model symptom to the MOST appropriate first remediation step.

skills: 2.1.1: Organizing different types of data, including tabular, text, speech, images, and videos, for efficient training.
questions.question:
The data engineering team is preparing 12 TB of labeled image data stored as individual JPEG files in Cloud Storage for distributed training of a custom TensorFlow model on Vertex AI. They observe that GPU utilization stays below 30% during training because of slow input pipeline throughput.

Which approach is the MOST effective way to organize the dataset to maximize training throughput?

choices.text: Convert the JPEG images and labels into sharded `TFRecord` files of roughly 100-200 MB each in Cloud Storage and read them with `tf.data.TFRecordDataset` using parallel interleave and prefetch.
choices.explanation: Sharded TFRecord files provide sequential reads, parallel I/O across shards, and high throughput suitable for distributed training.

choices.text: Compress all JPEG files into a single tar.gz archive in Cloud Storage and stream it directly into the training job using `tf.data.Dataset.from_generator`.
choices.explanation: A single archive serializes reads and prevents parallel I/O, making input throughput a hard bottleneck.

choices.text: Load the JPEG files individually with `tf.data.Dataset.list_files` and apply `num_parallel_reads=1` to ensure ordered reads from Cloud Storage.
choices.explanation: Reading millions of small files in serial from object storage is dominated by per-object latency and starves the GPU.

choices.text: Copy the JPEG files into a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL table as BYTEA columns and query batches over JDBC during training.
choices.explanation: Relational databases are not designed for high-throughput binary streaming and would severely cap input pipeline performance.

questions.tip: Think about how training pipelines achieve parallel I/O across many files in object storage.
questions.explanation:
Sharded binary record files are the canonical Vertex AI / TensorFlow pattern for high-throughput distributed training on large image corpora.

**Why it works:** Splitting data into ~100-200 MB shards lets `tf.data` read multiple shards in parallel, decode in parallel, and prefetch batches so the GPU is never idle waiting for data.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Single archive: serializes reads and defeats parallelism.
- Serial list_files: per-object latency dominates throughput.
- Cloud SQL BYTEA: relational storage is the wrong primitive for ML data pipelines.

skills: 2.1.1: Organizing different types of data, including tabular, text, speech, images, and videos, for efficient training.
questions.question:
The analytics team stores six years of transactional tabular data, around 4 TB, in a single BigQuery table. Data scientists frequently train models on rolling 90-day windows and report that training jobs spend most of their time scanning historical rows that are then filtered out.

What is the MOST cost-effective change to the table layout to support efficient model training?

choices.text: Partition the table by the transaction date column and cluster it on the customer segment column, then have training jobs query only the relevant partitions.
choices.explanation: Partition pruning eliminates scans of out-of-window data and clustering further reduces bytes scanned for segment filters.

choices.text: Export the entire table to CSV in Cloud Storage and have training jobs filter the rolling window in pandas before model fitting.
choices.explanation: CSV export forfeits BigQuery's columnar pruning and forces full-data downloads.

choices.text: Create a materialized view that selects all columns with no filter and point training jobs at the view.
choices.explanation: An unfiltered materialized view does not reduce scanned bytes for windowed training queries.

choices.text: Convert the table to a BigLake external table backed by Avro files in Cloud Storage with no partitioning.
choices.explanation: An unpartitioned external table still requires scanning all underlying files for time-windowed queries.

questions.tip: Consider how columnar warehouses prune data when training queries always filter by a known dimension.
questions.explanation:
Time-window training on warehouse data is exactly the workload BigQuery partitioning and clustering were designed for.

**Why it works:** Date partitioning lets BigQuery prune all partitions outside the 90-day window, and clustering on segment further reduces scanned bytes for segment filters.

**Why the others don't work:**
- CSV export: loses columnar pruning entirely.
- Unfiltered materialized view: still reads everything.
- Unpartitioned BigLake: external storage without partitioning provides no pruning.
questions.domain: Collaborating Within and Across Teams to Manage Data and Models

skills: 2.1.1: Organizing different types of data, including tabular, text, speech, images, and videos, for efficient training.
questions.question:
You are organizing a 25 TB collection of raw 4K surveillance videos in Cloud Storage to be used for training a video action recognition model on Vertex AI. The team needs predictable training throughput and reasonable storage costs over the multi-month training cycle.

Which TWO actions should you take to organize this dataset for efficient training?

choices.text: Pre-process videos into fixed-length clips at the target training resolution and frame rate, stored as sharded TFRecord or WebDataset tar shards in Cloud Storage.
choices.explanation: Pre-decoded, right-sized clips remove per-step decode cost and enable parallel sharded reads.

choices.text: Store the raw 4K videos and the training-ready clips in a Standard storage class bucket in the same region as the Vertex AI training job.
choices.explanation: Co-locating training data in the same region as compute avoids egress cost and minimizes I/O latency for hot training data.

choices.text: Move all videos to the Archive storage class to minimize storage cost during training.
choices.explanation: Archive class has retrieval latency and per-read costs that make it unsuitable for active training data.

choices.text: Keep each video as a single multi-gigabyte object and read it directly into the training loop with `cv2.VideoCapture`.
choices.explanation: Decoding huge videos at every step starves accelerators and prevents parallel reads.

choices.text: Load every clip into a Cloud Spanner table as BYTES and query Spanner during training.
choices.explanation: Spanner is a transactional database and is not designed for streaming bulk media to training jobs.

questions.tip: Think about both how data is shaped for the input pipeline and where it physically lives.
questions.explanation:
Efficient video training requires both the right serialization format and co-location with compute.

**Why it works:** Pre-cut clips in sharded record formats give parallel, sequential reads with cheap decode; placing those shards in the same region as the training cluster keeps I/O fast and free of egress cost.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Archive class: retrieval cost and latency break active training.
- Raw multi-GB videos: decode bottleneck and no parallelism.
- Spanner BYTES: wrong storage primitive for ML data.

skills: 2.1.2: Managing datasets in Vertex AI.
questions.question:
The MLOps team is centralizing image-classification datasets across three product groups. Each group has its own labeling vendor and produces JSONL annotation files plus images in Cloud Storage. The team wants a single managed catalog where datasets can be versioned, shared across projects, and consumed by both AutoML and custom training jobs.

Which approach should you adopt?

choices.text: Create Vertex AI managed image datasets, import each vendor's JSONL and images, and grant Vertex AI Dataset roles to consuming projects.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI managed datasets provide schema validation, versioning metadata, and IAM-controlled sharing across AutoML and custom training.

choices.text: Store the JSONL files in a shared Cloud Storage bucket and have each team write its own loader code per training job.

choices.text: Load all annotations into a Cloud SQL database and have training jobs query rows over JDBC.

questions.tip: Look for the native Vertex AI surface that represents a dataset as a first-class, governed resource.

Vertex AI managed datasets are the first-class catalog for image, text, video, and tabular training data.

skills: 2.1.2: Managing datasets in Vertex AI.
questions.question:

questions.explanation:
BigQuery is the native source for Vertex AI tabular datasets and avoids data duplication.

**Why it works:** A BigQuery URI source keeps the dataset consistent with the live table and removes export pipelines.

**Why the others don't work:**

skills: 2.1.2: Managing datasets in Vertex AI.
questions.question:
During a data-quality review, the team discovers that several Vertex AI image datasets contain duplicate images, mislabeled examples, and import errors that were never investigated. They want to add governance to dataset management going forward.

Which TWO actions support better dataset management within Vertex AI?

choices.text: Inspect the dataset's import error file in Cloud Storage and fix the JSONL rows before re-importing data items.

questions.tip: Think about both correcting bad rows and getting authoritative labels in.

Good Vertex AI dataset management combines fixing import errors and using labeling jobs for human-in-the-loop corrections.

**Why it works:** The error-file workflow handles malformed inputs while labeling jobs handle ambiguous content; both keep the managed dataset authoritative.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disabling IAM: destroys governance.
- Coldline: storage class is not governance.
- Deleting the dataset: throws away the managed surface entirely.

skills: 2.1.3: Applying data preprocessing techniques using tools such as Dataflow, TensorFlow Extended (TFX), and BigQuery.
questions.question:
The fraud team ingests roughly 40,000 events per second from Pub/Sub and needs to enrich, window, and aggregate features in near real time before writing them to BigQuery for both analytics and online model scoring. Latency from event arrival to feature availability must stay under one minute.

Which preprocessing approach is the MOST suitable?

choices.text: Run a streaming Dataflow pipeline that reads from Pub/Sub, applies windowed aggregations, and writes enriched features into BigQuery via the Storage Write API.
choices.explanation: Dataflow streaming with the Storage Write API is the canonical low-latency, high-throughput preprocessing path on Google Cloud.

choices.text: Schedule a BigQuery scheduled query every five minutes that reads raw events from a staging table and recomputes aggregations.
choices.explanation: Scheduled queries cannot meet the sub-minute latency target and reprocess data each run.

choices.text: Run a Cloud Run service per event that performs Python pandas aggregations and inserts rows into BigQuery via streaming inserts.
choices.explanation: Per-event Python pandas does not maintain windowed state and does not scale at 40k events per second.

choices.text: Use a Cloud Composer DAG that triggers every minute to run a Dataproc PySpark batch job over the last minute of data.
choices.explanation: Repeated micro-batch Dataproc jobs add scheduling overhead and stateful windowing is not native.

questions.tip: Match the throughput and latency constraint to the streaming-native preprocessing service.
questions.explanation:
Dataflow streaming is built for stateful, high-throughput, low-latency preprocessing.

**Why it works:** Apache Beam pipelines on Dataflow handle windowed aggregations, exactly-once writes via the Storage Write API, and autoscaling at the required event rate.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Scheduled query: latency floor too high.
- Per-event Cloud Run: stateless and not throughput-shaped.
- Composer + Dataproc micro-batch: scheduling overhead and no native windowing.

skills: 2.1.3: Applying data preprocessing techniques using tools such as Dataflow, TensorFlow Extended (TFX), and BigQuery.
questions.question:
The MLOps team is building a TFX pipeline on Vertex AI Pipelines for a fraud-scoring model. They want training-time normalization statistics, vocabularies, and bucket boundaries to be applied identically at serving time without rewriting code.

Which TFX component should they use?

choices.text: The `Transform` component, which uses `tf.Transform` to compute full-pass statistics on Dataflow and emit a `transform_graph` that is embedded in the served model.
choices.explanation: tf.Transform produces a graph of preprocessing ops that is fused into the SavedModel, eliminating training/serving skew.

choices.text: The `ExampleGen` component, configured with custom Python UDFs to compute bucket boundaries.
choices.explanation: ExampleGen ingests examples; it does not compute or persist transformation graphs.

choices.text: The `Trainer` component, with normalization computed inside the model's training loop on each step.
choices.explanation: Per-step normalization does not produce a reusable preprocessing graph and is recomputed every run.

choices.text: The `Evaluator` component, exporting normalization metrics into Vertex AI Metadata for the serving pipeline.
choices.explanation: Evaluator measures model quality; it does not export a preprocessing graph for serving.

questions.tip: Look for the component that produces a graph reused at both training and serving time.
questions.explanation:
TFX Transform is the canonical answer for preventing training/serving skew.

**Why it works:** Transform runs full-pass analyzers on Dataflow and emits a transform_graph that is embedded in the served model so the same ops execute at inference.

**Why the others don't work:**
- ExampleGen: ingestion, not transformation.
- Trainer in-loop: not reused at serving.
- Evaluator: measures models, not preprocessing.

skills: 2.1.3: Applying data preprocessing techniques using tools such as Dataflow, TensorFlow Extended (TFX), and BigQuery.
questions.question:
After reviewing quarterly spending, leadership asks the data team to keep tabular preprocessing inside BigQuery wherever possible to reduce data movement and cost. The team is preparing features for a churn model trained in Vertex AI.

Which TWO preprocessing techniques are appropriate to perform in BigQuery for this workflow?

choices.text: Compute aggregated time-window features (counts, sums, averages) per customer using SQL window functions and persist them to a feature table.
choices.explanation: BigQuery window functions are highly efficient for warehouse-scale aggregated feature computation.

choices.text: Bucketize numeric columns and one-hot encode low-cardinality categorical columns using SQL `CASE` and `ML.QUANTILE_BUCKETIZE` or `ML.ONE_HOT_ENCODER` transforms.
choices.explanation: BigQuery ML provides native preprocessing transforms that can be applied during query time and during inference.

choices.text: Decode and resize 4K video frames into 224x224 tensors using SQL UDFs.
choices.explanation: Video decoding is not appropriate in SQL and BigQuery is not a media processing engine.

choices.text: Train deep speech recognition models directly in BigQuery using audio waveform UDFs.
choices.explanation: BigQuery does not train deep ASR models on audio; this is a Vertex AI custom training workload.

choices.text: Stream live IoT sensor packets directly into BigQuery and run per-row UDFs that mutate Pub/Sub topics.
choices.explanation: Mutating Pub/Sub from BigQuery UDFs is not a supported preprocessing pattern.

questions.tip: Stay within the workloads BigQuery is designed to do well at warehouse scale.
questions.explanation:
Tabular feature engineering, aggregation, bucketization, and encoding are exactly what BigQuery handles natively at scale.

**Why it works:** SQL window functions and BigQuery ML transforms keep heavy tabular preprocessing in the warehouse without exporting data.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Video decode in SQL: wrong tool for media.
- Deep ASR in BigQuery: not a training surface for audio models.
- BigQuery UDFs mutating Pub/Sub: not a real preprocessing pattern.

skills: 2.1.4: Creating and consolidating features in Vertex AI Feature Store.
questions.question:
The platform team manages a curated BigQuery dataset of customer features that several model teams currently re-derive in their own pipelines. Leadership wants one consolidated source of features that supports both batch training and low-latency online lookups for real-time scoring.

Which approach BEST consolidates these features?

choices.text: Register the BigQuery feature tables as Vertex AI Feature Store feature groups and feature views, and serve them online through a feature online store with a sync schedule.
choices.explanation: Feature groups/views over BigQuery plus an online store deliver one canonical definition for batch and online use.

choices.text: Create per-team materialized views in BigQuery and expose them through Looker dashboards.
choices.explanation: Looker is for analytics consumption; it does not provide low-latency online feature serving for inference.

choices.text: Copy the BigQuery features into a Cloud Storage bucket as Parquet files and have each team load them into their training jobs.
choices.explanation: Parquet copies do not provide a managed registry, sync, or online serving surface.

choices.text: Provision a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance and replicate features from BigQuery hourly using Datastream.

questions.tip: Look for the managed surface that links a tabular source to both batch and online consumers.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Feature Store is the consolidated registry and serving layer for BigQuery-sourced features.

**Why it works:** Feature groups/views map BigQuery columns to feature definitions, while the online store handles low-latency serving and scheduled syncs.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Looker views: analytics surface only.
- Parquet copies: no registry or online path.

questions.question:
The recommendations team is preparing a low-latency online model deployed on Vertex AI Online Prediction. The model needs the latest values of 23 user features at inference, and they expect a sustained 5,000 QPS with a p99 latency budget of 30 ms for the feature lookup step.

Which serving configuration is the MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Configure a Bigtable-backed online feature store with a feature view fed by a BigQuery source on a periodic sync.
choices.explanation: Bigtable online stores deliver consistent single-digit millisecond reads at high QPS, suitable for the latency budget.

choices.text: Read features at inference time directly from BigQuery using `bigquery.Client().query()` for each request.

choices.text: Run feature aggregations from raw event tables on every prediction request via a Dataflow pipeline.

High-QPS, low-latency online feature serving is what Bigtable-backed Vertex AI online feature stores are designed for.

skills: 2.1.4: Creating and consolidating features in Vertex AI Feature Store.
questions.question:
You are designing how multiple teams will collaborate on a shared Vertex AI Feature Store. You want to ensure features are consolidated, governed, and reusable rather than re-implemented per project.

Which TWO actions should you take to support this consolidation?

choices.text: Define a single set of feature groups per business entity (for example, user, product, transaction) backed by canonical BigQuery tables and shared across teams.
choices.explanation: Entity-aligned feature groups give every team one canonical definition per entity.

choices.text: Use feature views to compose features from one or more feature groups for specific model consumers, and grant IAM access at the view level.
choices.explanation: Feature views let teams compose entity features without duplicating definitions, while IAM controls who consumes which view.

choices.text: Allow each team to create overlapping feature groups using their own BigQuery copies of the same source tables.
choices.explanation: Overlapping definitions break the single-source-of-truth goal and reintroduce drift.

choices.text: Disable feature monitoring so that producer teams are not slowed down by data drift alerts.
choices.explanation: Disabling monitoring removes the governance signal that keeps shared features trustworthy.

choices.text: Replicate every feature value into a separate Cloud Spanner database per team for isolation.
choices.explanation: Per-team replication into Spanner reintroduces silos and removes the consolidated registry.

questions.tip: Think about both the canonical definition and how it is shared without duplication.
questions.explanation:
Consolidation comes from canonical entity-level feature groups plus shared feature views with IAM.

**Why it works:** Feature groups give one definition per entity; feature views let downstream teams pick what they need without copying source data.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Overlapping team copies: defeats consolidation.
- Disabling monitoring: removes governance.
- Per-team Spanner copies: replays the silo problem.

skills: 2.1.5: Identifying privacy implications of data usage and collection, including handling sensitive data such as PII and PHI.
questions.question:
The healthcare analytics team needs to share a BigQuery training dataset with a partner data-science team. The dataset contains patient names, addresses, and free-text clinician notes. Legal requires that direct identifiers be removed while preserving the analytic value of the records, including referential consistency across rows.

Which approach BEST meets these requirements?

choices.text: Run Sensitive Data Protection de-identification on the table using format-preserving encryption with a tokenization key for direct identifiers and `infoType` redaction inside the free-text notes.
choices.explanation: FPE tokenization keeps referential consistency, and infoType-based redaction removes free-text identifiers.

choices.text: Apply a SQL `REPLACE()` function to overwrite values containing the substring 'name' or 'address' with empty strings.
choices.explanation: Substring rewriting misses many real PII patterns and gives false confidence.

choices.text: Hash all string columns with `SHA256` so that no original values are recoverable.
choices.explanation: Bulk hashing destroys analytic value and still allows reidentification of low-entropy fields.

choices.text: Use BigQuery column-level access controls to hide identifier columns from the partner team's role.
choices.explanation: Column-level ACLs hide columns but do not address identifiers embedded in free-text notes.

questions.tip: The free-text fields are the hardest part; choose a service designed to find and transform PII inside them.
questions.explanation:
Sensitive Data Protection (formerly Cloud DLP) is purpose-built for finding and transforming PII at scale.

**Why it works:** FPE tokenization preserves joins across rows while removing the original value, and infoType detectors find PII embedded in clinician notes.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Substring REPLACE: misses real PII.
- Bulk SHA256: destroys utility, vulnerable to dictionary attacks for low-entropy values.
- Column ACLs alone: ignore PII inside free-text.
questions.domain: Collaborating Within and Across Teams to Manage Data and Models

skills: 2.1.5: Identifying privacy implications of data usage and collection, including handling sensitive data such as PII and PHI.
questions.question:
During a privacy review, you must produce a defensible inventory of where PII actually lives across hundreds of Cloud Storage buckets and BigQuery datasets used by ML teams. The current process relies on team-submitted spreadsheets that legal considers unreliable.

Which is the MOST appropriate first step?

choices.text: Run Sensitive Data Protection discovery scans across the Cloud Storage buckets and BigQuery datasets to produce an automated, evidenced inventory of `infoTypes` and their locations.
choices.explanation: Automated discovery produces an evidenced inventory based on actual content rather than self-reporting.

choices.text: Send a new mandatory survey to every team and consolidate the responses into a central spreadsheet.
choices.explanation: Self-reported surveys are exactly what legal already considers unreliable.

choices.text: Enable Cloud Audit Logs on storage and warehouse APIs and infer PII presence from access patterns.
choices.explanation: Audit logs show access, not content; they cannot identify PII presence.

choices.text: Encrypt all buckets and datasets with customer-managed keys and assume PII is now adequately handled.
choices.explanation: CMEK protects data at rest but does not identify or inventory PII.

questions.tip: The unreliability of the current process is the clue; you need automated content evidence.
questions.explanation:
Sensitive Data Protection discovery is the canonical first step for a content-based PII inventory.

**Why it works:** Discovery scans introspect actual contents and emit findings into a structured inventory legal can defend.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Surveys: same self-reporting failure mode.
- Audit logs: no content visibility.
- CMEK: encryption is not classification.
questions.domain: Collaborating Within and Across Teams to Manage Data and Models

skills: 2.1.5: Identifying privacy implications of data usage and collection, including handling sensitive data such as PII and PHI.
questions.question:
Management has decided that any ML pipeline ingesting data that may contain PII or PHI must enforce privacy controls at both rest and in transit, with auditable key ownership.

Which TWO controls should be configured to meet this requirement?

choices.text: Encrypt the Cloud Storage buckets, BigQuery datasets, and Vertex AI resources with customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) managed in Cloud KMS.
choices.explanation: CMEK provides auditable key ownership and rotation across the data and ML stack.

choices.text: Run Sensitive Data Protection de-identification as a step in the ingestion pipeline before data lands in any training dataset.
choices.explanation: Pre-training de-identification ensures sensitive identifiers never reach the training surface in the first place.

choices.text: Disable all VPC Service Controls perimeters so security tooling can read data freely.
choices.explanation: Disabling VPC-SC removes a key data-exfiltration boundary and weakens privacy posture.

choices.text: Grant `Editor` role at the project level to anyone working on the ML pipeline.
choices.explanation: Broad Editor grants violate least privilege and undermine auditable handling of PII/PHI.

choices.text: Store identifiers in plaintext in a single shared Cloud Storage bucket so all teams can see them.
choices.explanation: Plaintext shared identifiers are the failure mode the policy is intended to prevent.

questions.tip: Combine an encryption-at-rest control with an upstream content control.
questions.explanation:
Privacy controls combine encryption with key ownership and content de-identification before training.

**Why it works:** CMEK addresses rest and key custody; SDP de-identification addresses content sensitivity before it spreads.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disabling VPC-SC: removes exfil boundary.
- Project Editor: violates least privilege.
- Plaintext shared identifiers: explicit policy violation.
questions.domain: Collaborating Within and Across Teams to Manage Data and Models

They want a managed pathway that handles parsing, chunking, embedding, and retrieval at inference time without building bespoke pipeline code.

choices.text: Use Vertex AI RAG Engine to import the Cloud Storage corpus, which handles parsing, chunking, embedding, and retrieval, and reference the corpus from Gemini at inference.
choices.explanation: RAG Engine is the managed corpus ingestion and retrieval surface tied directly into Gemini grounding.

choices.explanation: This rebuilds RAG from scratch and conflicts with the requirement to avoid bespoke pipeline code.

choices.text: Fine-tune a Gemini model on every PDF and DOCX file so all knowledge is internalized in the model weights.

choices.text: Upload all documents into a Vertex AI image dataset and reference them from the model.
choices.explanation: Image datasets are not the ingestion surface for text grounding.

questions.tip: Look for the managed end-to-end ingestion and retrieval surface for text grounding.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI RAG Engine is the managed path for ingesting text corpora into Gemini grounding.

**Why it works:** RAG Engine handles parsing, chunking, embedding, indexing, and retrieval without custom pipeline code.

**Why the others don't work:**
- DIY Dataflow + Cloud SQL: bespoke, exactly what the team wants to avoid.

questions.tip: Match the workload to the managed ANN service designed for it.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Vector Search is the managed approximate nearest neighbor index for production retrieval.

**Why it works:** It scales to billions of vectors, gives millisecond ANN latency, and integrates with Vertex AI endpoints for retrieval-augmented inference.

skills: 2.2.2: Applying security best practices in Vertex AI Workbench.
questions.question:
Following a security review, a regulated financial services team must ensure that Vertex AI Workbench instances cannot reach the public internet and that data exchanged with Google APIs stays on Google's network. The team also wants to prevent data exfiltration of training datasets stored in Cloud Storage.

Which combination provides the MOST secure network configuration?

choices.text: Deploy Workbench instances with no external IP, enable Private Google Access on the subnet, and place the project inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter that includes Cloud Storage and Vertex AI APIs.
choices.explanation: Removing external IPs, enabling Private Google Access, and using VPC Service Controls together prevent internet egress and data exfiltration.

choices.text: Assign Workbench instances external IPs and rely on hierarchical firewall policies to deny outbound traffic to all CIDRs except Google API IP ranges.
choices.explanation: Maintaining external IPs and IP-allowlist firewall rules is fragile and does not enforce service-level perimeter controls.

choices.text: Enable Cloud NAT for the subnet and rotate the NAT IP weekly, while restricting Cloud Storage buckets with bucket-level uniform access.
choices.explanation: Cloud NAT still permits internet egress, and uniform bucket access does not stop authorized identities from exfiltrating data.

choices.text: Place Workbench instances on the default network and use organization policy to require OS Login while leaving public Google API endpoints accessible.
choices.explanation: The default network is permissive, OS Login does not address data exfiltration, and public API endpoints are still reachable.

questions.tip: Combine network isolation with a service-level perimeter to control both connectivity and data movement.
questions.explanation:
Removing external IPs, using Private Google Access, and wrapping the project in a VPC Service Controls perimeter is the documented secure configuration.

**Why it works:** Traffic stays on Google's backbone, and the perimeter blocks data movement outside trusted projects.

**Why the others don't work:**
- External IP plus firewall allowlist: brittle and does not stop service-level exfiltration.
- Cloud NAT: still permits outbound internet traffic.
- Default network plus OS Login: does not address exfiltration risk.

skills: 2.2.2: Applying security best practices in Vertex AI Workbench.
questions.question:
The platform engineering group is hardening Vertex AI Workbench instances used by data scientists handling regulated PHI. They need to guarantee that boot integrity is verified and that all persistent disks are encrypted with keys managed by the security team rather than Google-managed keys.

What is the recommended configuration?

choices.text: Create Workbench instances with Shielded VM secure boot and vTPM enabled, and specify a customer-managed encryption key from Cloud KMS for the boot and data disks.
choices.explanation: Shielded VM features verify boot integrity, and a CMEK ensures the security team controls disk encryption keys.

choices.text: Use the default Google-managed encryption keys and rely on Cloud HSM to attest to boot integrity at runtime.
choices.explanation: Google-managed keys do not give the security team direct control, and Cloud HSM does not attest to VM boot integrity.

choices.text: Enable confidential computing on the instance and store training data only in BigQuery to bypass disk encryption requirements.
choices.explanation: Confidential computing addresses memory protection, not boot integrity, and BigQuery does not eliminate disk encryption requirements for the VM.

choices.text: Encrypt notebooks client-side with a passphrase before saving them to the local disk on the Workbench instance.
choices.explanation: Client-side passphrase encryption does not provide boot integrity verification or centrally managed key control.

questions.tip: Consider both VM boot integrity and key ownership when securing instance disks.
questions.explanation:
Shielded VM features combined with a Cloud KMS CMEK provide the documented hardening posture.

**Why it works:** Secure boot and vTPM verify integrity at startup, and CMEK gives the security team key lifecycle control.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Google-managed keys plus Cloud HSM: does not deliver customer key control or boot attestation.
- Confidential computing only: addresses memory, not boot or disk key ownership.
- Client-side passphrase: ad hoc and not centrally manageable.

skills: 2.2.2: Applying security best practices in Vertex AI Workbench.
questions.question:
Management has decided to enforce least-privilege and reduce the attack surface of Vertex AI Workbench instances used by a large data science organization. Auditors have flagged long-running idle notebooks and over-privileged service accounts as concerns.

Which TWO practices should the team adopt?

choices.text: Attach a dedicated user-managed service account with only the IAM roles required for the workload to each Workbench instance.
choices.explanation: User-managed service accounts allow least-privilege scoping per project or team rather than using the broad default Compute Engine service account.

choices.text: Configure idle shutdown on Workbench instances so that idle notebooks are automatically stopped after a defined period.
choices.explanation: Idle shutdown reduces exposure of running notebooks and limits cost when researchers stop using the instance.

choices.text: Grant the Editor role on the project to all data scientists so they can self-service any required permission.
choices.explanation: Editor is broadly privileged and contradicts least-privilege principles.

choices.text: Disable Cloud Audit Logs on Workbench API methods to reduce log storage costs in a centralized SIEM.
choices.explanation: Disabling audit logs removes the ability to investigate misuse, weakening security posture.

choices.text: Allow third-party JupyterLab extensions from any source to be installed by end users without administrator review.
choices.explanation: Unreviewed third-party extensions can introduce supply chain risk and data exfiltration paths.

questions.tip: Think about identity scoping and runtime exposure together.
questions.explanation:
Dedicated service accounts and idle shutdown both shrink the attack surface in line with documented best practices.

**Why it works:** Per-instance service accounts enforce least privilege, and idle shutdown removes idle long-running compute.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Project Editor for all users: violates least privilege.
- Disabling audit logs: removes detective controls.
- Unreviewed extensions: introduces supply chain risk.

choices.text: Deploy the Llama model from its Model Garden card to a Vertex AI endpoint with a managed serving container.
choices.explanation: Model Garden one-click deploy uses managed serving containers and Vertex AI endpoints, minimizing operational work.

choices.text: Have the application call the Vertex AI endpoint, abstracting the underlying model so it can be swapped later.

choices.text: Build and maintain a bespoke Triton Inference Server cluster on Google Kubernetes Engine for the Llama model.
choices.explanation: A bespoke cluster increases operational overhead unnecessarily.

choices.text: Have the application load the Llama weights directly from Cloud Storage on every request and run inference in process.

choices.text: Hard-code the specific Llama version into client SDK calls so future swaps require client redeployment.

questions.tip: Combine the managed deploy path with an abstraction that supports future change.
questions.explanation:

**Why it works:** Managed serving handles infrastructure, and the endpoint hides the model identity from the client.

**Why the others don't work:**

- Per-request weight loading: inefficient.
- Hard-coded model in clients: blocks future swaps.

questions.question:

They want a managed environment to track parameters, metrics, and dataset versions across runs while also visualizing scalar loss curves and weight histograms during training. The team is small and wants minimal infrastructure setup.

Which Google Cloud combination is the MOST suitable for this workflow?

choices.text: Use Vertex AI Experiments to log runs, parameters, and metrics, and integrate Vertex AI TensorBoard for visualizing scalars, histograms, and graphs during TensorFlow training
choices.explanation: Vertex AI Experiments tracks runs and metadata while Vertex AI TensorBoard provides the visualization layer for TensorFlow summaries.

choices.text: Deploy a self-managed MLflow tracking server on Google Kubernetes Engine and stream TensorFlow event files to a Cloud Storage bucket for manual inspection
choices.explanation: This adds operational overhead and lacks an integrated TensorBoard visualization experience.

choices.text: Use Kubeflow Pipelines on a user-managed cluster to orchestrate every training run and store metrics in BigQuery for ad hoc SQL analysis
choices.explanation: Kubeflow Pipelines is designed for orchestration of end-to-end workflows, not lightweight experiment tracking and scalar visualization.

choices.text: Run training in a Vertex AI Workbench notebook and rely on local matplotlib charts saved to the notebook for run comparison
choices.explanation: Local plots cannot reliably compare runs across team members or capture detailed training metrics.

questions.tip: Consider which managed services are purpose-built for run tracking versus deep training visualization.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Experiments centralizes run metadata while Vertex AI TensorBoard handles deep training visualization. Together they remove infrastructure management for the team.

**Why it works:** Vertex AI Experiments captures parameters, metrics, and lineage per run, and the integrated TensorBoard backing store renders the TF summary writers natively.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Self-managed MLflow: introduces cluster maintenance and lacks TensorBoard integration.
- Kubeflow Pipelines + BigQuery: pipeline orchestration is heavier than needed and BigQuery is not a training visualizer.
- Notebook with matplotlib: not collaborative and misses scalar/histogram tooling.

skills: 2.3.2: Evaluating generative AI solutions.
questions.question:
The applied AI team at a customer support SaaS provider has fine-tuned a Gemini model to summarize tickets. They need to systematically compare the fine-tuned model against the base model on a held-out dataset using both reference-based metrics like ROUGE and model-based metrics for fluency and groundedness. The team prefers a managed approach.

Which approach is the BEST fit?

choices.text: Use the Vertex AI Gen AI Evaluation Service with computation-based and model-based metrics on the evaluation dataset, comparing both candidate models in a single evaluation run
choices.explanation: The Gen AI Evaluation Service supports side-by-side computation and model-based metrics in a managed workflow.

choices.text: Export both models to Cloud Storage and run a custom Python harness on a Compute Engine VM that calls scikit-learn metrics over the predictions
choices.explanation: scikit-learn does not provide model-based generative metrics like groundedness, and self-hosting adds overhead.

choices.text: Use BigQuery ML `ML.EVALUATE` on inference outputs stored in BigQuery to compute generative metrics
choices.explanation: `ML.EVALUATE` targets supervised metrics for tabular models, not generative model evaluation.

choices.text: Generate predictions with both models and rely solely on a manual spot-check of 20 outputs to choose the better model
choices.explanation: Manual spot-checks at this scale are not statistically reliable and do not produce comparable metrics.

questions.tip: Consider which managed service is purpose-built for generative model evaluation on Google Cloud.
questions.explanation:
The Gen AI Evaluation Service in Vertex AI handles both reference-based and model-based metrics for generative outputs in a managed pipeline.

**Why it works:** It is designed to evaluate and compare generative models with metrics including ROUGE, BLEU, fluency, coherence, and groundedness.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Custom scikit-learn harness: lacks generative metrics like groundedness.
- BigQuery ML `ML.EVALUATE`: not for generative LLM outputs.
- Manual spot-check: not systematic or repeatable.
questions.domain: Collaborating Within and Across Teams to Manage Data and Models

skills: 2.3.2: Evaluating generative AI solutions.
questions.question:
After reviewing quarterly spending, leadership at a legal-tech startup wants quantitative confidence that a Retrieval-Augmented Generation chatbot built on Vertex AI is grounding its answers in the provided document corpus rather than hallucinating. The evaluation must use a labeled set of questions paired with reference documents.

Which evaluation metric should the team prioritize?

choices.text: A groundedness metric that measures whether generated responses are supported by the provided reference context
choices.explanation: Groundedness directly measures faithfulness to the supplied context, which is the team's stated concern.

choices.text: Perplexity computed on the model's token distribution over the answer
choices.explanation: Perplexity measures language modeling quality, not factual grounding in retrieved context.

choices.text: Mean Average Precision over the top-k retrieved chunks from the vector index
choices.explanation: MAP evaluates retrieval quality but does not assess whether the generator faithfully uses the context.

choices.text: BLEU score between the response and the user's original question
choices.explanation: Comparing response to question is not meaningful, and BLEU is reference-translation oriented.

questions.tip: Map the business concern about hallucination to the metric that names that property.
questions.explanation:
Groundedness measures whether the model's output is supported by the supplied context, which is exactly the property leadership wants to verify.

**Why it works:** It compares each generated claim against the reference passages and flags unsupported claims.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Perplexity: measures fluency, not factual support.
- Retrieval MAP: only evaluates the retriever, not the final response.
- BLEU vs question: a category mismatch.
questions.domain: Collaborating Within and Across Teams to Manage Data and Models

skills: 2.3.2: Evaluating generative AI solutions.
questions.question:
The engineering team is evaluating a generative AI assistant before launch. They want a robust evaluation strategy that combines automated scoring with human judgment, and that can be re-run on each model release.

Which TWO practices should be part of the evaluation pipeline?

choices.text: Curate a versioned evaluation dataset with diverse, representative prompts and store it in Cloud Storage so each release runs against the same benchmark
choices.explanation: A stable, versioned dataset enables reproducible comparisons across releases.

choices.text: Combine automated metrics from the Gen AI Evaluation Service with periodic human ratings for nuanced criteria like helpfulness and tone
choices.explanation: Automated and human evaluation are complementary for generative quality.

choices.text: Re-use the training data as the evaluation dataset to maximize coverage of the model's strengths
choices.explanation: Evaluating on training data leaks the train set and overstates performance.

choices.text: Rely entirely on the average user star rating from production traffic, with no offline evaluation
choices.explanation: Production-only evaluation cannot gate releases or compare candidates pre-launch.

choices.text: Tune the evaluation rubric on each release to make the new model score higher than the previous one
choices.explanation: Changing the rubric per release destroys comparability and biases results.

questions.tip: Think about reproducibility and the limits of automated metrics for subjective qualities.
questions.explanation:
A stable evaluation set plus a hybrid of automated and human review is the standard approach for generative AI release gating.

**Why it works:** Reproducibility comes from a fixed dataset and rubric, while human judgment captures qualities that metrics miss.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Reusing training data: data leakage.
- Star ratings only: not pre-launch and not controlled.
- Tuning the rubric per release: invalidates comparisons.
questions.domain: Collaborating Within and Across Teams to Manage Data and Models

skills: 3.1.1: Choosing the appropriate ML framework and model architecture.
questions.question:

They need to scale training to a 200 GB dataset on Google Cloud while keeping their existing scikit-learn pipeline almost unchanged and minimizing engineering effort.

Which approach is the MOST suitable for productionizing this prototype?

choices.text: Package the scikit-learn training script into a custom container and submit it as a Vertex AI custom training job using a prebuilt scikit-learn container image
choices.explanation: Vertex AI offers prebuilt scikit-learn containers that run the existing pipeline at scale with minimal code changes.

choices.text: Rewrite the entire pipeline in TensorFlow Estimators and submit it to Vertex AI Training using a prebuilt TensorFlow container
choices.explanation: Rewriting in TensorFlow adds significant engineering effort and is unnecessary for a tabular scikit-learn workflow.

choices.text: Convert the scikit-learn model into an XGBoost model and run distributed training on Dataproc with the Spark MLlib library
choices.explanation: Converting frameworks and switching to MLlib introduces large rewrites and changes the underlying algorithm semantics.

choices.text: Export the dataset to BigQuery and rebuild the model using BigQuery ML LOGISTIC_REG without using scikit-learn at all
choices.explanation: BigQuery ML requires reformulating the model in SQL and abandoning the existing scikit-learn pipeline.

questions.tip: Consider which option preserves the existing framework while leveraging managed scale.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI custom training jobs support prebuilt containers for popular frameworks including scikit-learn.

**Why it works:** A prebuilt scikit-learn container lets the team submit their existing training script as a managed job with high CPU/memory resources, scaling without rewriting the pipeline.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Rewriting in TensorFlow: unnecessary effort for tabular scikit-learn code.
- Converting to XGBoost on Dataproc: changes both framework and algorithm.
- Rebuilding in BigQuery ML: abandons the existing prototype entirely.

- Scikit-learn ResNet: framework cannot represent deep CNNs.

skills: 3.1.2: Applying modeling techniques given interpretability requirements.
questions.question:
A bank is deploying a credit-risk model on Vertex AI and regulators require per-prediction feature attributions for each loan decision. The team has trained a deep neural network in TensorFlow on tabular features and must surface attributions to compliance reviewers without retraining the model.

Which approach is the MOST appropriate to satisfy the interpretability requirement?

choices.text: Deploy the TensorFlow model to a Vertex AI endpoint with Vertex Explainable AI configured to return integrated gradients attributions for each online prediction
choices.explanation: Integrated gradients is well suited to differentiable TensorFlow models and surfaces per-prediction attributions through the endpoint.

choices.text: Replace the deep neural network with a logistic regression model in BigQuery ML and rely on the model coefficients as global attributions
choices.explanation: This requires retraining and provides only global, not per-prediction, attributions.

choices.text: Enable Vertex AI Model Monitoring feature drift detection and present the drift dashboards to regulators
choices.explanation: Drift monitoring measures data shifts, not per-prediction feature contributions.

choices.text: Wrap predictions in Cloud Functions that compute Pearson correlations between inputs and outputs at request time
choices.explanation: Correlations are not valid feature attributions and do not capture model behavior.

questions.tip: Focus on per-prediction explanations available without changing the model.
questions.explanation:
Vertex Explainable AI integrates with deployed models to deliver feature attributions for each prediction.

**Why it works:** Integrated gradients computes path-based attributions for differentiable models and is exposed through the explain method on Vertex AI endpoints.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Logistic regression replacement: changes the model and only gives global coefficients.
- Model Monitoring drift: addresses data shift, not interpretability.
- Cloud Functions correlations: not a valid attribution method.

skills: 3.1.2: Applying modeling techniques given interpretability requirements.
questions.question:
The fraud team is choosing a model for a tabular fraud-detection use case where investigators need to understand which features drove every flagged transaction. Training data and predictions both live in BigQuery, and the team prefers to avoid managing custom training infrastructure.

Which modeling choice BEST balances predictive performance with the interpretability requirement?

choices.text: Train a BigQuery ML boosted tree classifier and use ML.EXPLAIN_PREDICT to return per-row Shapley feature attributions alongside predictions
choices.explanation: BigQuery ML's ML.EXPLAIN_PREDICT returns Shapley-based attributions for boosted tree and other models, all within SQL.

choices.text: Train a deep autoencoder in TensorFlow on Vertex AI and use reconstruction error as the explanation for each flagged transaction
choices.explanation: Reconstruction error is a single anomaly score and does not identify which features drove a decision.

choices.text: Train a k-means clustering model in BigQuery ML and present the cluster ID as the explanation
choices.explanation: Cluster IDs do not provide feature-level attributions for individual predictions.

choices.text: Use AutoML Tables and disclose only the global feature importance chart without per-prediction explanations
choices.explanation: Global importance does not satisfy a per-transaction interpretability requirement.

questions.tip: Look for a model that pairs strong tabular performance with built-in per-prediction attributions.
questions.explanation:
BigQuery ML boosted tree models combine strong tabular accuracy with native Shapley explanations.

**Why it works:** ML.EXPLAIN_PREDICT exposes per-row Shapley values directly in SQL, satisfying both the platform and interpretability constraints.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Autoencoder reconstruction error: not a feature attribution.
- k-means clusters: no per-feature explanation.
- AutoML global importance only: misses per-prediction needs.

skills: 3.1.2: Applying modeling techniques given interpretability requirements.
questions.question:
The healthcare ML team is preparing to deploy an image-based diagnostic model trained on Vertex AI. Clinical reviewers must see which regions of each input image contributed most to the model's prediction, and the team wants to use built-in Vertex AI explainability features rather than custom code.

Which TWO Vertex Explainable AI feature attribution methods are appropriate for this image model?

choices.text: Configure integrated gradients attributions which highlight pixel contributions for differentiable image models
choices.explanation: Integrated gradients is supported for image models served on Vertex AI endpoints.

choices.text: Configure XRAI attributions which provide region-based saliency tailored for natural images
choices.explanation: XRAI is designed specifically for image models and produces region-level attributions.

choices.text: Configure sampled Shapley attributions because they are the only method supported for image models on Vertex AI
choices.explanation: Sampled Shapley is intended for tabular non-differentiable models, not images.

choices.text: Enable confidence calibration to expose softmax temperature as the explanation signal
choices.explanation: Calibration adjusts probabilities and is not a feature attribution method.

choices.text: Replace the model with k-means clustering on image embeddings to derive cluster-level explanations
choices.explanation: Clustering does not produce per-image region attributions.

questions.tip: Consider attribution methods designed for image inputs.
questions.explanation:
Vertex Explainable AI supports both integrated gradients and XRAI for image models.

**Why it works:** Both methods compute pixel or region-level attributions for differentiable image models without custom implementation.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Sampled Shapley: targeted at tabular models.
- Confidence calibration: not an attribution technique.
- k-means on embeddings: provides no per-prediction region attributions.

skills: 3.1.2: Applying modeling techniques given interpretability requirements.
questions.question:
The MLOps team is enabling per-prediction feature attributions for an existing tabular TensorFlow model on Vertex AI.

Arrange the following steps in the correct order to deliver explanations to consumers.

choices.text: Identify interpretability requirements and select an attribution method such as sampled Shapley or integrated gradients
choices.explanation: Choosing the method first ensures the model and metadata align with stakeholder needs.

choices.text: Define explanation metadata describing input and output tensors when uploading the model to the Vertex AI Model Registry
choices.explanation: Explanation metadata must be attached when registering the model so the platform knows which tensors to attribute.

choices.text: Deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint with explanation configuration enabled
choices.explanation: Deployment with explanation config is required before serving explanations.

choices.text: Call the explain method on the endpoint and surface attributions to downstream reviewers
choices.explanation: The explain method returns per-prediction attributions to the consuming application.

questions.tip: Think about which decision must precede registration and deployment.
questions.explanation: Interpretability requirements drive method choice, which informs metadata at registration, deployment configuration, and finally request-time explanation calls.

skills: 3.2.1: Organizing training data types, including tabular, text, speech, images, and videos, on Google Cloud using Cloud Storage and BigQuery.
questions.question:
The data engineering team at a retail analytics firm is preparing tens of millions of structured customer transaction rows for use as training data for a churn prediction model in Vertex AI. They need fast SQL-based feature engineering, schema enforcement, and the ability to materialize feature snapshots for repeatable training runs.

Which storage approach is the MOST suitable for this tabular workload?

choices.text: Land the transaction data in BigQuery tables and run feature engineering with SQL, producing versioned snapshot tables that Vertex AI training jobs read directly through the BigQuery connector.
choices.explanation: BigQuery is the canonical store for large structured tabular training data and integrates natively with Vertex AI training and feature engineering workflows.

choices.text: Export each daily batch of transactions to per-row JSON objects in a Cloud Storage bucket with autoclass enabled and load them into the training job as a streaming dataset.
choices.explanation: Per-row JSON in Cloud Storage is inefficient for large structured tabular data and loses schema enforcement, schema evolution, and SQL feature engineering benefits.

choices.text: Persist the transactions in Bigtable using a tall-narrow row key design and have the Vertex AI training job perform full table scans for every epoch.
choices.explanation: Bigtable is optimized for low-latency lookups, not scan-heavy SQL feature engineering or repeatable tabular training snapshots.

choices.text: Store the transactions in Firestore in Native mode and have the training job use the client library to iterate documents during each training step.
choices.explanation: Firestore is a document database for application state and is not designed for scan-oriented tabular ML training workloads.

questions.tip: Consider which Google Cloud service is purpose-built for analytical SQL over large tabular datasets.
questions.explanation:
BigQuery is the right home for analytical, schema-enforced tabular training data that requires SQL feature engineering and versioned snapshots.

**Why it works:** BigQuery offers columnar storage, schema enforcement, partitioning, time-travel snapshots, and a first-class Vertex AI integration so training jobs can read tabular features directly without expensive exports.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Per-row JSON in Cloud Storage loses schema and is inefficient for tabular data.
- Bigtable is for low-latency key lookups, not analytical scans.
- Firestore is a document store for application data, not ML training scans.

skills: 3.2.1: Organizing training data types, including tabular, text, speech, images, and videos, on Google Cloud using Cloud Storage and BigQuery.
questions.question:
The computer vision team is building an image classification model in Vertex AI using a dataset of approximately 12 million labeled images stored on premises. They want to upload the images to Google Cloud once, organize them so labels are easy to derive, and avoid the small-file penalty during training.

Which approach to organizing the images on Cloud Storage is BEST?

choices.text: Upload the images to a regional Cloud Storage bucket grouped under per-class prefixes, then convert the dataset into sharded TFRecord files in the same bucket for the training job to stream.
choices.explanation: Per-class prefixes give a clean labeling structure, and sharded TFRecord files solve the small-file throughput issue during training.

choices.text: Upload the raw images to a multi-region Cloud Storage bucket with no prefixes and rely on a separate metadata file in Firestore to map each object to its label at training time.
choices.explanation: Looking up labels in Firestore for each image during training adds latency and external dependencies; a metadata-only approach scales poorly and ignores small-file overhead.

choices.text: Store every image as a base64 string in a BigQuery column alongside its label so the training job can issue SQL queries for each batch.
choices.explanation: BigQuery is not optimized for binary blob storage or row-by-row image fetching during training and would be slow and expensive.

choices.text: Place the images in Filestore Basic HDD instances mounted into the training cluster and rely on directory names for labels.
choices.explanation: Filestore is optimized for NFS workloads inside a VPC and is not the recommended storage tier for large-scale image training pipelines on Vertex AI.

questions.tip: Think about how directory structure can encode labels and how large datasets are typically packaged for high-throughput training.
questions.explanation:
Organizing image training data by per-class prefixes and packaging it into sharded TFRecord files is the standard pattern for scalable Vertex AI image training.

**Why it works:** Prefix-based organization makes label derivation trivial, and sharded record files dramatically reduce per-object overhead during high-throughput training reads.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Firestore label lookups add latency and a brittle dependency.
- BigQuery is not a binary blob store.
- Filestore is not the recommended tier for this scale of training data.

skills: 3.2.1: Organizing training data types, including tabular, text, speech, images, and videos, on Google Cloud using Cloud Storage and BigQuery.
questions.question:
You are designing the data layout for a multimodal training pipeline that combines structured customer profile data with raw audio recordings of support calls. The team wants the layout to follow Google Cloud best practices for ML training storage.

Which TWO actions should you take?

choices.text: Store the structured customer profile features in BigQuery so they can be joined and engineered with SQL before being exported as training inputs.
choices.explanation: BigQuery is the recommended store for structured tabular features used in ML pipelines.

choices.text: Store the raw audio files in a regional Cloud Storage bucket co-located with the Vertex AI training region.
choices.explanation: Cloud Storage is the recommended store for large unstructured media, and co-locating with the training region minimizes egress and latency.

choices.text: Store the raw audio files as BYTES columns in BigQuery alongside the structured features so a single table backs the entire training set.
choices.explanation: BigQuery is not designed for large binary blobs like audio recordings; this approach is expensive and inefficient.

choices.text: Store the structured customer profile features as one JSON file per customer in Cloud Storage to keep all training data on the same service.
choices.explanation: Storing structured features as small JSON files loses BigQuery's schema and SQL benefits and creates small-file scaling problems.

choices.text: Place all audio files in a multi-region Cloud Storage bucket in a different continent from the training region to maximize redundancy.
choices.explanation: Reading large training datasets from a distant region introduces high latency and unnecessary cost; co-location is preferred for training.

questions.tip: Match each modality to the Google Cloud service it is designed for.
questions.explanation:
Structured features belong in BigQuery; large unstructured media like audio belongs in regional Cloud Storage co-located with the training job.

**Why it works:** This split uses each service for the data shape it is optimized for and keeps the training job close to its data.

**Why the others don't work:**
- BigQuery is not designed for storing raw audio blobs.
- Splitting structured data across many JSON files in Cloud Storage forfeits SQL-based feature engineering.
- Cross-continent reads from a multi-region bucket harm training throughput and cost.
