skills: 5.1.7: Designing systems using TFX components or Kubeflow DSL including Dataflow.
questions.question:
The ML engineering team is designing a TFX pipeline that processes hundreds of millions of training examples. They want the ExampleGen, StatisticsGen, and Transform components to scale horizontally on a managed runner without provisioning a cluster.

Which runner configuration is MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Configure the TFX components to use the Dataflow runner for Apache Beam, allowing the heavy data processing steps to autoscale on a managed service.
choices.explanation: Beam-based TFX components run on Dataflow with autoscaling and no cluster management.

choices.text: Set the Beam runner to DirectRunner so each component runs in the local Vertex AI Pipelines container.
choices.explanation: DirectRunner runs in a single process and cannot scale horizontally to large datasets.

choices.text: Run the TFX components on a manually provisioned Spark cluster on Compute Engine to maximize tuning flexibility.
choices.explanation: Self-managed Spark adds operational burden and is not the recommended TFX scaling path.

choices.text: Disable horizontal scaling and rely on a single very large Compute Engine VM to process the data sequentially.
choices.explanation: Vertical scaling alone cannot match the throughput of a distributed Beam runner.

questions.tip: Look for the Apache Beam runner that scales managed and serverless on Google Cloud.
questions.explanation:
Dataflow is the recommended Beam runner for scaling TFX components.

**Why it works:** TFX's Beam components delegate to Dataflow for autoscaling, parallel processing on Google Cloud.

**Why the others don't work:**
- DirectRunner: single process, not scalable.
- Manual Spark: high ops cost.
- Single VM: cannot scale horizontally.

skills: 5.1.7: Designing systems using TFX components or Kubeflow DSL including Dataflow.
questions.question:
During design review, the team is selecting TFX components to validate features and gate model promotion. They want to enforce a quality bar relative to the currently deployed model and reject any candidate that performs worse on key slices.

Which TFX component combination achieves this?

choices.text: Use the Evaluator component with an `EvalConfig` that defines metric thresholds and a baseline model, and add the Pusher component conditioned on the Evaluator's blessing.
choices.explanation: Evaluator emits a blessing artifact that Pusher consumes to decide whether to push the new model.

choices.text: Use only the Trainer component and rely on the training loss being lower than the previous run before deployment.
choices.explanation: Training loss alone does not validate against the deployed champion or sliced metrics.

choices.text: Use the SchemaGen component to generate a new schema after training and reject deployment when the schema changes.
choices.explanation: SchemaGen handles data structure, not model quality.

choices.text: Use the Transform component to compare new and old features and only push when feature distributions match exactly.
choices.explanation: Transform applies feature engineering and is not a model evaluation gate.

questions.tip: Identify the component that produces a blessing artifact based on metric thresholds.
questions.explanation:
Evaluator and Pusher together implement the standard TFX champion-challenger gate.

**Why it works:** Evaluator outputs a blessing decision based on the EvalConfig that Pusher consumes to gate deployment.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Trainer alone: no champion comparison.
- SchemaGen: schema, not metrics.
- Transform: preprocessing, not evaluation.

skills: 5.1.7: Designing systems using TFX components or Kubeflow DSL including Dataflow.
questions.question:
The platform team is authoring a Vertex AI Pipelines workflow using the Kubeflow Pipelines v2 DSL. They want their pipeline to be modular, parameterizable, and able to delegate heavy data preparation to a scalable runner.

Which TWO authoring practices align with these goals?

choices.text: Author reusable lightweight Python components using the `@dsl.component` decorator and compose them inside an `@dsl.pipeline` definition with typed parameters.
choices.explanation: Decorator-based components and parameters yield modular, parameterizable pipelines.

choices.text: Implement heavy data preparation as an Apache Beam job that runs on Dataflow and invoke it from a pipeline component using the Dataflow runner.
choices.explanation: Delegating heavy work to Dataflow keeps the pipeline component lightweight while scaling data processing.

choices.text: Inline all logic into a single monolithic component to keep the pipeline simple and avoid intermediate artifact serialization.
choices.explanation: Monolithic components defeat modularity and prevent reuse.

choices.text: Hard-code dataset locations and hyperparameters inside each component to make pipelines self-contained.
choices.explanation: Hard-coded values break parameterization and prevent reuse across environments.

choices.text: Run all heavy preprocessing inside the pipeline orchestrator container itself with a single CPU and no autoscaling.
choices.explanation: The orchestrator container is not designed for large-scale data processing.

questions.tip: Look for modular component design and offloading heavy work to a managed runner.
questions.explanation:
KFP v2 DSL components plus Dataflow for heavy lifting is the canonical authoring pattern on Vertex AI Pipelines.

**Why it works:** Decorator components are reusable and parameterizable; Dataflow scales the heavy data preparation.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Monolithic components: not modular.
- Hard-coded values: not parameterizable.
- Orchestrator-side processing: not scalable.

skills: 5.2.1: Determining an appropriate retraining policy.
questions.question:
The data science team at a logistics company has deployed a delivery time prediction model to a Vertex AI endpoint. Customer behavior changes seasonally and the team wants retraining to happen automatically only when input feature distributions shift meaningfully from the training baseline, rather than on a fixed schedule.

Which approach provides the MOST appropriate retraining trigger?

choices.text: Configure a Vertex AI Model Monitoring job for feature skew and drift detection on the endpoint, then use the resulting alert to trigger a Vertex AI Pipelines retraining run via Pub/Sub and Cloud Functions.
choices.explanation: Drift detection on the live endpoint is the canonical signal for condition-based retraining and integrates cleanly with Pipelines via Pub/Sub.

choices.text: Schedule a daily Cloud Scheduler job that retrains the model regardless of incoming traffic, ensuring the model is always rebuilt with the latest BigQuery data.
choices.explanation: A fixed daily cadence wastes compute when no drift exists and is the opposite of a condition-based policy.

choices.text: Enable continuous evaluation only, comparing prediction accuracy against ground truth labels every hour, and trigger retraining whenever a single hourly batch shows lower accuracy than the previous one.
choices.explanation: Hour-to-hour accuracy fluctuation is noisy, ground truth is rarely available that quickly for delivery times, and this ignores feature distribution shifts.

choices.text: Use Cloud Logging metrics on endpoint request count to trigger retraining whenever request volume rises above a threshold, treating traffic spikes as a proxy for distribution change.
choices.explanation: Request volume is unrelated to feature distribution and would retrain during marketing surges where the underlying data has not shifted.

questions.tip: Think about which signal directly reflects whether the model's input world has changed.
questions.explanation:
Feature skew and drift detection in Vertex AI Model Monitoring measures statistical distance between live inputs and the training baseline, which is exactly what a condition-based retraining policy needs.

**Why it works:** Model Monitoring computes drift metrics on production traffic and emits alerts to Pub/Sub, which can launch a Vertex AI Pipelines retraining run only when the data has actually moved.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Fixed daily schedule: ignores whether drift has occurred and wastes resources.
- Hourly accuracy comparison: ground truth lag and noise make this unreliable.
- Request count threshold: traffic volume does not indicate feature distribution change.

skills: 5.2.1: Determining an appropriate retraining policy.
questions.question:
The marketing analytics team retrains a churn prediction model every Monday morning using the previous week of behavioral data from BigQuery. Labels are reliably available within 48 hours and the team wants the simplest possible managed retraining cadence with minimal operational overhead.

Which retraining policy is the BEST fit?

choices.text: Create a recurring schedule on the Vertex AI Pipelines training pipeline using the built-in scheduler, configured for weekly execution on Monday at the desired time.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI Pipelines has a native recurring schedule resource that matches a fixed weekly cadence with no extra infrastructure.

choices.text: Stand up a Compute Engine VM running cron, install the Vertex AI SDK, and trigger pipeline runs from a shell script every Monday.
choices.explanation: A self-managed VM adds patching and uptime concerns that the managed scheduler eliminates.

choices.text: Deploy a Cloud Run service that polls BigQuery every five minutes for new rows and starts a pipeline run whenever the row count exceeds a threshold.
choices.explanation: Polling logic and a custom threshold are far more operational overhead than a weekly cadence requires.

choices.text: Configure Vertex AI Model Monitoring with skew detection and only retrain when drift alerts fire, ignoring the weekly business cadence.
choices.explanation: Drift-based retraining does not align with the team's stated weekly cadence requirement and adds monitoring complexity that is not needed.

questions.tip: Match the retraining mechanism to the cadence the business actually wants.
questions.explanation:
When a fixed cadence is desired and labels arrive on a predictable timeline, the managed Vertex AI Pipelines schedule resource is the lowest-effort option.

**Why it works:** A pipeline schedule is a fully managed cron-like resource that launches the same pipeline definition on a recurring basis without any additional compute.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Compute Engine cron: reintroduces VM management.
- Cloud Run polling: adds custom logic for a problem already solved by the schedule resource.
- Drift-only retraining: contradicts the explicit weekly business requirement.

skills: 5.2.1: Determining an appropriate retraining policy.
questions.question:
You are designing a hybrid retraining policy for a fraud detection model deployed on a Vertex AI endpoint. The team wants retraining to occur both when prediction quality degrades and when upstream feature distributions change, while still capping the maximum interval between retrains.

Which TWO components should form the core of this policy?

choices.text: A Vertex AI Model Monitoring job configured for both feature drift and prediction drift, emitting Pub/Sub alerts that start a retraining pipeline run.
choices.explanation: Combining feature and prediction drift covers both input change and output behavior change.

choices.text: A scheduled Vertex AI Pipelines run that fires on a maximum interval such as monthly, ensuring retraining happens even when no drift is detected.
choices.explanation: A maximum-interval schedule guarantees the model never goes stale during quiet periods.

choices.text: A Cloud Functions trigger that retrains the model whenever a new row is written to the source BigQuery table, regardless of volume.
choices.explanation: Per-row retraining is wasteful and would retrain thousands of times per day with no business benefit.

choices.text: A manual approval gate in the Google Cloud console that requires an engineer to click a button before any retraining begins.
choices.explanation: Manual approval is not a retraining trigger and adds latency without ensuring drift coverage or interval caps.

choices.text: A static accuracy threshold computed once at deployment and hardcoded into the serving container, with retraining triggered if live accuracy ever dips below it.
choices.explanation: Hardcoding thresholds in the container couples model logic to retraining policy and bypasses the managed monitoring service.

questions.tip: Hybrid policies usually pair an event-based signal with a time-based safety net.
questions.explanation:
A robust retraining policy combines drift-based triggers with a maximum interval schedule.

**Why it works:** Model Monitoring covers feature and prediction drift events, while a scheduled Pipelines run guarantees a refresh cadence even when no drift is observed.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Per-row Cloud Functions: triggers are too frequent and not aligned with policy intent.
- Manual approval gate: not a trigger mechanism.
- Hardcoded threshold in container: bypasses managed monitoring and is brittle.

skills: 5.2.1: Determining an appropriate retraining policy.
questions.question: Match each retraining trigger scenario to the Google Cloud mechanism that best implements it.

slots.label: Retrain only when live input feature distributions diverge from the training baseline
Retrain on a fixed weekly cadence aligned to a business reporting cycle

skills: 5.2.2: Implementing CI/CD model deployment pipelines using Cloud Build and Jenkins.
questions.question:
The platform team is building a CI/CD pipeline that deploys a custom training container to a Vertex AI endpoint whenever a pull request merges into the main branch of a Cloud Source Repositories repo. They want native integration with the repository, container builds stored in Artifact Registry, and minimal third-party tooling.

Which pipeline design is the MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Configure a Cloud Build trigger on push to main that builds the container, pushes it to Artifact Registry, then runs a `gcloud ai models upload` and `gcloud ai endpoints deploy-model` step in the same `cloudbuild.yaml`.
choices.explanation: Cloud Build natively triggers on Cloud Source Repositories pushes and can chain build, push, and Vertex AI deploy steps in one config.

choices.text: Run a Jenkins server on a Compute Engine VM that polls Cloud Source Repositories every minute, builds the image locally on the agent, and uses scp to copy it to Vertex AI.
choices.explanation: Polling is inefficient and Vertex AI does not accept scp, models must come from Artifact Registry.

choices.text: Use Cloud Functions to listen for repository commits, run docker build inside the function runtime, and call the Vertex AI REST API to upload the model.
choices.explanation: Cloud Functions cannot perform container builds in their runtime and have memory and time limits unsuited to image builds.

choices.text: Configure a Cloud Build trigger but have it write the source to Cloud Storage, then rely on a Cloud Scheduler job to pick up the source nightly and deploy it to Vertex AI.
choices.explanation: Inserting nightly batching breaks CI/CD continuous delivery semantics and removes the link between commit and deploy.

questions.tip: Look for the option that keeps build, registry, and deploy inside Google Cloud managed services.
questions.explanation:
Cloud Build is the native CI/CD service on Google Cloud and integrates directly with Cloud Source Repositories, Artifact Registry, and Vertex AI deployment commands.

**Why it works:** A single `cloudbuild.yaml` can build the image, push to Artifact Registry, and call `gcloud ai endpoints deploy-model` on commit.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Self-managed Jenkins with polling and scp: outdated and incompatible with Vertex AI artifact handling.
- Cloud Functions for docker build: not a supported pattern.
- Nightly batched deploys: breaks the CI/CD trigger relationship.

skills: 5.2.2: Implementing CI/CD model deployment pipelines using Cloud Build and Jenkins.
questions.question:
Your organization already runs a corporate Jenkins controller and wants to keep using it for ML model CI/CD, but your existing Compute Engine Jenkins agents struggle to scale with parallel build demand. You want ephemeral, isolated build agents that scale on demand within Google Cloud.

Which approach provides the LEAST operational overhead while keeping Jenkins as the orchestrator?

choices.text: Run Jenkins on Google Kubernetes Engine using the Kubernetes plugin so each build spawns an ephemeral agent pod, pushing images to Artifact Registry and deploying to Vertex AI from the pipeline.
choices.explanation: GKE-hosted Jenkins with ephemeral agent pods is the documented pattern for scalable Jenkins on Google Cloud.

choices.text: Add more permanent Compute Engine Jenkins agent VMs and let them sit idle between builds to avoid cold-start delays.
choices.explanation: Idle VMs increase cost and operational toil and do not scale dynamically.

choices.text: Replace Jenkins entirely with Cloud Build, even though the requirement is to keep Jenkins as the orchestrator.
choices.explanation: This contradicts the explicit requirement to retain Jenkins.

choices.text: Run all Jenkins builds on the controller node itself by setting executor count to a high number, eliminating agents.
choices.explanation: Builds on the controller exhaust controller resources and is an anti-pattern in Jenkins documentation.

questions.tip: Consider where ephemeral, autoscaling compute lives natively in Google Cloud.
questions.explanation:
The reference architecture for Jenkins on Google Cloud places the controller on GKE and uses the Kubernetes plugin to launch a pod per build.

**Why it works:** Each build gets a clean pod, Kubernetes handles scheduling and scaling, and pods terminate when the build ends, removing manual agent management.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Idle VM agents: costly and not autoscaling.
- Replacing Jenkins: violates the stated constraint.
- Running on the controller: degrades stability and is discouraged.

skills: 5.2.2: Implementing CI/CD model deployment pipelines using Cloud Build and Jenkins.
questions.question:
The MLOps team is hardening a Cloud Build pipeline that builds a custom prediction container, registers a Vertex AI Model, and deploys it to a Vertex AI endpoint. They want a safe rollout that limits blast radius if the new model performs poorly in production.

Which TWO actions should be included in the `cloudbuild.yaml` to support a safer deployment?

choices.text: Deploy the new Vertex AI Model version to the existing endpoint with a low `traffic_split` such as 10 percent, leaving the prior version on the remaining traffic.
choices.explanation: Traffic splitting on a Vertex AI endpoint is the canonical way to canary new model versions.

choices.text: Add a build step that runs a batch evaluation job against a held-out dataset and fails the build if metrics regress beyond a threshold before traffic shifts.
choices.explanation: Gating deploy on automated evaluation prevents bad models from reaching the endpoint at all.

choices.text: Delete the previous deployed model from the endpoint immediately after pushing the new container image so only one version exists at a time.
choices.explanation: Removing the old version eliminates the ability to roll back instantly and increases blast radius.

choices.text: Disable IAM checks on the Cloud Build service account during deploy steps to reduce the chance of permission errors halting the pipeline.
choices.explanation: Disabling IAM checks is unsafe and unrelated to model rollout safety.

choices.text: Skip Artifact Registry and have Cloud Build push container images straight to a personal developer's Container Registry project.
choices.explanation: Bypassing the central registry breaks auditability and is not a safer deployment mechanism.

questions.tip: Think about gating before deploy and limiting traffic during deploy.
questions.explanation:
Safer rollouts combine pre-deploy validation with progressive traffic shifting.

**Why it works:** Batch evaluation acts as a quality gate before the endpoint sees the model, and a small initial traffic split contains impact if it does misbehave in production.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Deleting the old version: removes rollback capacity.
- Disabling IAM checks: never a safer pattern.
- Pushing to personal registry: breaks supply chain controls.

skills: 5.2.2: Implementing CI/CD model deployment pipelines using Cloud Build and Jenkins.
questions.question: Following a merge to the main branch, a Cloud Build pipeline must build, register, and deploy a custom prediction container to a Vertex AI endpoint. Arrange the pipeline steps in the correct order.

choices.text: Build the prediction container image from the source in the repository
choices.explanation: The image must exist before it can be pushed or referenced.

choices.text: Push the built image to Artifact Registry
choices.explanation: Vertex AI Model Registry imports containers from Artifact Registry, not from local build context.

choices.text: Upload the model to the Vertex AI Model Registry referencing the Artifact Registry image
choices.explanation: Registration must precede endpoint deployment.

choices.text: Deploy the registered model version to the Vertex AI endpoint with the configured traffic split
choices.explanation: Endpoint deployment is the final step and references the registered model resource.

questions.tip: Consider which artifact each step depends on from the previous one.
questions.explanation: A CI/CD model deployment pipeline must build, push, register, and then deploy in that order because each step consumes the output of the previous one.

skills: 5.3.1: Tracking and comparing model artifacts and versions using Vertex AI Experiments and Vertex ML Metadata.
questions.question:
The data science team at a fintech company is iterating on a credit risk model and running dozens of training jobs per week with different hyperparameters, feature sets, and base models. They need a side by side comparison of input parameters, evaluation metrics, and the resulting model artifacts so they can decide which run to promote to staging.

Which approach provides the MOST suitable solution with the least custom tooling?

choices.text: Wrap each training run in a Vertex AI Experiments run, log parameters and metrics with `aiplatform.log_params` and `aiplatform.log_metrics`, and compare runs in the Experiments console.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI Experiments is purpose-built for tracking parameters, metrics, and artifacts and offers a built-in run comparison view.

choices.text: Write each run's parameters and metrics to a BigQuery table from the training container, then build a Looker Studio dashboard to compare runs.
choices.explanation: This works but requires significant custom plumbing and does not natively link to model artifacts or lineage.

choices.text: Stream training logs to Cloud Logging with structured payloads, then query them with Log Analytics to compare each run's outputs.
choices.explanation: Cloud Logging is for operational logs, not structured experiment tracking, and lacks artifact and lineage integration.

choices.text: Save TensorBoard event files to Cloud Storage from each job and open them locally with the open source TensorBoard CLI for comparison.
choices.explanation: Local TensorBoard does not centralize parameters, artifacts, or lineage and provides no managed comparison UI tied to model versions.

questions.tip: Look for the managed feature that natively records inputs, metrics, and artifacts together.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Experiments is the managed Google Cloud service designed for this exact workflow.

**Why it works:** Each `ExperimentRun` captures parameters, metrics, and artifact references, and the Experiments UI provides direct multi-run comparison without custom code.

**Why the others don't work:**
- BigQuery + Looker Studio: Functional but custom and decoupled from artifacts and lineage.
- Cloud Logging: Designed for operational logs, not structured ML experiment tracking.
- Local TensorBoard: No managed comparison or artifact linkage across runs.

skills: 5.3.1: Tracking and comparing model artifacts and versions using Vertex AI Experiments and Vertex ML Metadata.
questions.question:
During an audit of a Vertex AI Pipelines workflow, the MLOps lead is asked to demonstrate exactly which dataset version, preprocessing component, and training step produced the model that was deployed last quarter. The pipeline emits standard KFP component outputs.

Which Google Cloud capability should be used to retrieve the connected graph of artifacts and executions?

choices.text: Query Vertex ML Metadata using the Metadata Store APIs to traverse the lineage graph linking the model artifact back through executions to the source dataset artifact.
choices.explanation: Vertex ML Metadata stores artifact, execution, and context entities and exposes a queryable lineage graph for pipelines.

choices.text: Open the Cloud Storage bucket where pipeline outputs are written and inspect the folder structure to reconstruct the dataset and model relationships.
choices.explanation: Folder layout is not a reliable lineage source and does not capture executions or component relationships.

choices.text: Use Cloud Asset Inventory to list all Vertex AI resources at the time of deployment and infer which dataset was used.
choices.explanation: Cloud Asset Inventory tracks resource configuration history but does not record ML artifact lineage between dataset and model.

choices.text: Re-run the pipeline with the same parameters and assume identical artifacts were produced previously.
choices.explanation: Re-running does not recover historical lineage and depends on non-deterministic data sources matching.

questions.tip: Pipelines automatically write artifact and execution records into a managed lineage store.
questions.explanation:
Vertex ML Metadata is the lineage backbone for Vertex AI Pipelines.

**Why it works:** Pipeline executions automatically register artifacts (datasets, models) and executions in the Metadata Store, enabling traversal from a deployed model back to its source data and processing steps.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cloud Storage layout: Not authoritative lineage and easily diverges from reality.
- Cloud Asset Inventory: Tracks resource state, not ML artifact relationships.
- Re-running: Cannot reconstruct historical lineage of a past deployment.

skills: 5.3.1: Tracking and comparing model artifacts and versions using Vertex AI Experiments and Vertex ML Metadata.
questions.question:
The research team at a healthcare startup is comparing several variations of a transformer-based classifier. They want both per-epoch training curves and a summary table of final hyperparameters and metrics for every candidate, all visible to collaborators in the Google Cloud console.

Which TWO actions together provide the MOST complete tracking and comparison setup?

choices.text: Initialize an Experiment with `aiplatform.init(experiment=...)` and call `aiplatform.start_run()` per run to log parameters, metrics, and a model artifact reference.
choices.explanation: This populates the Experiments comparison view with parameters, metrics, and linked artifacts.

choices.text: Attach a Vertex AI TensorBoard instance to the Experiment and stream training scalars from each run for time-series visualization.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI TensorBoard integrates with Experiments to provide rich per-step training curves alongside the summary view.

choices.text: Persist all run metadata as JSON files in Cloud Storage and rely on a custom static site for browsing.
choices.explanation: Custom storage and rendering bypass managed comparison features and lack collaborator access controls.

choices.text: Send metrics over Pub/Sub to a Dataflow job that writes them to Firestore for the team to query.
choices.explanation: This is a complex custom pipeline that duplicates capabilities already provided by Experiments and TensorBoard.

choices.text: Use Cloud Monitoring custom metrics to track training loss per run and review them in Metrics Explorer.
choices.explanation: Cloud Monitoring is for operational metrics and does not associate values with model artifacts or experiment runs.

questions.tip: Combine the experiment tracker with the visualization service designed to plug into it.
questions.explanation:
Pairing Experiments with Vertex AI TensorBoard delivers both the tabular summary and the curve visualizations the team needs.

**Why it works:** Experiments captures parameters, metrics, and artifacts per run, while TensorBoard gives interactive scalar/histogram views attached to those runs.

**Why the others don't work:**
- JSON in Cloud Storage: Custom and not integrated with the console.
- Pub/Sub + Dataflow + Firestore: Over-engineered duplication of managed services.
- Cloud Monitoring: Operational telemetry, not experiment tracking.

skills: 5.3.1: Tracking and comparing model artifacts and versions using Vertex AI Experiments and Vertex ML Metadata.
questions.question:
An ML engineer is instrumenting a Python training script so each run is captured in Vertex AI Experiments and the resulting model is later promoted to a registered version.

Arrange the following actions in the correct order.

choices.text: Call `aiplatform.init` with a project, location, and experiment name.
choices.explanation: Initializing the SDK with an experiment name scopes subsequent runs to that experiment.

choices.text: Start a run with `aiplatform.start_run` and log parameters and metrics during training.
choices.explanation: An active run is required before parameters, metrics, and artifacts can be associated with it.

choices.text: Log the trained model artifact path to the run and end the run.
choices.explanation: Recording the artifact closes out the run with a reference to the produced model.

choices.text: Compare runs in the Experiments console and upload the chosen model to Vertex AI Model Registry as a new version.
choices.explanation: Promotion happens after comparison selects the best run, registering its artifact as a versioned model.

questions.tip: Configuration precedes run scope, which precedes logging, which precedes promotion.
questions.explanation: Experiment tracking begins with SDK initialization, runs are then opened to capture parameters, metrics, and artifacts, and finally a winning run's model is registered.

skills: 5.3.2: Hooking into model and dataset versioning workflows.
questions.question:
The platform team at a logistics company wants every newly trained model to be registered as a new version of an existing model entry, with aliases like `default` and `staging` controlling which version is served by online endpoints. They need a single source of truth for model versions across teams.

Which approach BEST satisfies these requirements?

choices.text: Upload each trained artifact to Vertex AI Model Registry as a new version of the parent model and manage promotion using version aliases.
choices.explanation: Model Registry natively supports parent models, immutable versions, and aliases for promotion.

choices.text: Save each trained model as a uniquely named folder in Cloud Storage and update a config file that endpoints read at deploy time.
choices.explanation: Cloud Storage folders provide no managed version semantics, no aliases, and no integration with deployment APIs.

choices.text: Tag container images of each model in Artifact Registry and rely on image tags as version identifiers.
choices.explanation: Artifact Registry versions container images, not ML model entities with metadata, schemas, and aliases.

choices.text: Store model metadata rows in a Cloud SQL table and have CI/CD scripts query the latest row before deployment.
choices.explanation: This is custom infrastructure that duplicates capabilities of Model Registry and lacks deep Vertex AI integration.

questions.tip: Look for the managed registry built specifically for ML model versions and aliases.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Model Registry is purpose-built for versioning ML models.

**Why it works:** Each upload becomes a new version under the same parent model, and aliases (default, staging, etc.) move freely between versions to control which is active.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cloud Storage folders: No managed semantics for versions or aliases.
- Artifact Registry tags: Versions container images, not model entities.
- Cloud SQL custom table: Reinvents an existing managed service.

skills: 5.3.2: Hooking into model and dataset versioning workflows.
questions.question:
The data engineering team curates labeled image collections that are retrained on each quarter. They need each curated snapshot to be reproducible so that a future training pipeline can reference the exact set of labeled examples used at any point in time.

Which approach provides the MOST reliable dataset versioning hook into Vertex AI training?

choices.text: Create a new Vertex AI managed Dataset for each snapshot and reference it by resource ID from the training pipeline, while keeping immutable backing files in versioned Cloud Storage paths.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI managed Datasets give a stable resource ID, and immutable Cloud Storage paths guarantee the underlying files do not change.

choices.text: Mutate a single Vertex AI Dataset in place each quarter and rely on the dataset name to identify the current version.
choices.explanation: In-place mutation destroys reproducibility because past training runs cannot recover prior contents.

choices.text: Store all images under one Cloud Storage prefix without object versioning and pass the prefix into training jobs.
choices.explanation: Without object versioning or immutable layout, the contents at the prefix can drift between runs.

choices.text: Embed the labels directly into image filenames and overwrite the same files quarterly so consumers always read the latest labels.
choices.explanation: Overwriting destroys history, and filename-encoded labels are fragile and not a managed dataset abstraction.

questions.tip: Reproducibility requires both an immutable artifact and a stable identifier to reference it.
questions.explanation:
A new managed Dataset per snapshot, backed by immutable Cloud Storage paths, gives stable references for future runs.

**Why it works:** Pipelines pin to a specific Dataset resource, and Cloud Storage path immutability ensures the underlying images and labels never change.

**Why the others don't work:**
- In-place mutation: Breaks reproducibility entirely.
- Single prefix without versioning: Contents can drift silently.
- Overwriting filenames: Loses history and is not a managed abstraction.

skills: 5.3.2: Hooking into model and dataset versioning workflows.
questions.question:
An MLOps team wants their CI/CD process to automatically register a new model version whenever a training pipeline succeeds, without disrupting the version currently serving production traffic. Promotion to production should be a deliberate, auditable step.

Which TWO practices should be combined?

choices.text: Have the pipeline upload the trained model to Vertex AI Model Registry as a new version under the same parent model, leaving the existing default alias unchanged.
choices.explanation: This adds a version without affecting the alias that drives production routing.

choices.text: Use a separate Cloud Build trigger, gated by an approval, to move the `default` alias from the previous version to the new version.
choices.explanation: Manual approval on alias movement provides the deliberate, auditable promotion step.

choices.text: Configure the training pipeline to immediately overwrite the default alias on each successful run.
choices.explanation: Auto-promotion eliminates the deliberate gate and risks deploying unverified models to production.

choices.text: Delete the previous model version after each new upload to keep the registry small.
choices.explanation: Deleting prior versions removes rollback options and breaks audit history.

choices.text: Encode promotion status in the model display name and have endpoints parse names to decide which to load.
choices.explanation: Display names are not authoritative and bypass the alias mechanism designed for this purpose.

questions.tip: Separate "register" from "promote" with distinct steps and controls.
questions.explanation:
Continuous registration with gated alias movement gives both automation and safety.

**Why it works:** New versions appear automatically for inspection, and the production alias only moves under explicit approval, preserving rollback through prior versions.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Auto-overwriting alias: No deliberate gate.
- Deleting old versions: Loses rollback and history.
- Display name parsing: Bypasses managed promotion.

skills: 5.3.2: Hooking into model and dataset versioning workflows.
questions.question: Match each versioning concern to the Google Cloud capability that addresses it.

slots.label: Maintain multiple immutable iterations of a deployable model under one logical name
Move a stable pointer like `default` between successive model versions
Reference a curated, labeled training corpus by stable resource ID
Preserve historical contents of an underlying training file when overwrites occur

choices.text: Vertex AI Model Registry versions
choices.explanation: Each upload creates a new immutable version under the parent model.

choices.text: Vertex AI Model Registry version aliases
choices.explanation: Aliases provide stable, movable pointers to a chosen version.

choices.text: Vertex AI managed Datasets
choices.explanation: Managed Datasets expose stable resource IDs that pipelines can pin to.

choices.text: Cloud Storage object versioning
choices.explanation: Object versioning retains prior generations of an object after overwrite or delete.

questions.tip: Distinguish artifact identity, pointer movement, dataset identity, and file-level history.

skills: 5.3.3: Managing model and data lineage.
questions.question:
Following a regulator's request, the compliance team needs to demonstrate, for any deployed Vertex AI model, the exact upstream BigQuery dataset, preprocessing component, and training step that produced it. Pipelines today are authored with the Kubeflow Pipelines SDK and run on Vertex AI Pipelines.

Which solution requires the LEAST additional engineering effort?

choices.text: Rely on the lineage graph automatically captured by Vertex ML Metadata for pipeline executions and query it through the console or the Metadata API.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI Pipelines automatically writes artifact and execution records to Vertex ML Metadata, producing a queryable lineage graph.

choices.text: Add custom Python code to every component that writes upstream and downstream artifact references into a Spanner table.
choices.explanation: This duplicates lineage capture that Vertex ML Metadata already performs and adds maintenance burden.

choices.text: Enable Cloud Audit Logs Data Access logs on Vertex AI and reconstruct lineage by joining log entries.
choices.explanation: Audit logs record API calls, not artifact-to-execution-to-artifact relationships needed for lineage.

choices.text: Export pipeline run YAML files to Cloud Storage and parse them to reconstruct dependencies between steps.
choices.explanation: Run definitions show wiring at authoring time but not the runtime artifact identities and versions.

questions.tip: Vertex AI Pipelines feeds a managed lineage store automatically.
questions.explanation:
Vertex ML Metadata is automatically populated by Vertex AI Pipelines.

**Why it works:** Each component execution registers its input and output artifacts as nodes and edges, allowing traversal from any model back through preprocessing to source data.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Custom Spanner table: Reinvents an existing capability.
- Audit logs: Capture API calls, not artifact lineage.
- YAML parsing: Reflects definitions, not runtime artifact identities.

skills: 5.3.3: Managing model and data lineage.
questions.question:
An analytics platform feeds a Vertex AI feature store from BigQuery tables that are themselves built from raw Cloud Storage exports through scheduled BigQuery jobs and Dataflow transforms. The data governance team wants a single, cross-product view of how raw files become feature values consumed by ML models.

Which approach is the MOST suitable?

choices.text: Enable Dataplex data lineage so that BigQuery and Dataflow operations automatically populate a unified lineage graph that links Cloud Storage objects, BigQuery tables, and downstream consumers.
choices.explanation: Dataplex provides cross-service data lineage capture with native BigQuery and Dataflow integration.

choices.text: Use Vertex ML Metadata as the sole lineage system and rely on it to capture both BigQuery transformations and Dataflow jobs.
choices.explanation: Vertex ML Metadata captures pipeline-level ML artifacts, not native BigQuery and Dataflow data lineage.

choices.text: Have each Dataflow job emit lineage events to Cloud Logging and build a custom graph database from log queries.
choices.explanation: Custom log-based graph construction is fragile and re-implements managed lineage.

choices.text: Track all transformations through INFORMATION_SCHEMA views in BigQuery and infer Cloud Storage origins from query history.
choices.explanation: INFORMATION_SCHEMA exposes BigQuery internals but does not reach Dataflow or Cloud Storage objects.

questions.tip: When lineage spans data products beyond ML pipelines, look for the cross-service governance feature.
questions.explanation:
Dataplex data lineage is the cross-service offering for BigQuery, Cloud Storage, and Dataflow.

**Why it works:** Lineage is captured automatically at the source-system level and surfaced as a unified graph that complements ML pipeline lineage in Vertex ML Metadata.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Vertex ML Metadata alone: Bounded to ML pipelines, not generic data transforms.
- Custom log-based graph: Maintenance heavy and incomplete.
- INFORMATION_SCHEMA only: Limited to BigQuery scope.

skills: 5.3.3: Managing model and data lineage.
questions.question:
The MLOps team is designing end-to-end lineage for a recommendation system that ingests events into BigQuery, trains models in Vertex AI Pipelines, and serves them through Vertex AI Endpoints. They need both data lineage and model lineage available to auditors.

Which TWO actions should be part of the design?

choices.text: Enable Dataplex data lineage on the project so BigQuery and supporting transforms publish lineage automatically.
choices.explanation: Dataplex covers the data side of the lineage graph across BigQuery and related services.

choices.text: Author training as Vertex AI Pipelines with typed component artifacts so Vertex ML Metadata records dataset, model, and execution lineage.
choices.explanation: Typed artifacts in Vertex AI Pipelines automatically populate the ML Metadata lineage graph.

choices.text: Manually keep a spreadsheet of which dataset trained which model and update it after each release.
choices.explanation: Spreadsheets cannot guarantee accuracy or scale and have no API access for auditors.

choices.text: Disable artifact tracking in pipelines to reduce metadata storage costs.
choices.explanation: Disabling tracking removes the data needed to satisfy lineage requirements.

choices.text: Replace Vertex AI Endpoints with custom GKE serving so lineage can be inferred from Kubernetes labels.
choices.explanation: Kubernetes labels do not represent ML lineage and would force reinventing managed capabilities.

questions.tip: Cover both halves: data lineage via Dataplex and ML lineage via pipeline metadata.
questions.explanation:
Combining Dataplex with Vertex ML Metadata yields end-to-end lineage from raw data to served model.

**Why it works:** Dataplex captures data product lineage, while Vertex ML Metadata captures the ML-specific artifact and execution graph from pipeline runs, together giving auditors a complete picture.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Spreadsheet: Manual, error prone, not API queryable.
- Disabling tracking: Removes the very lineage data required.
- GKE labels: Not a lineage mechanism.

skills: 5.3.3: Managing model and data lineage.
questions.question:
An auditor asks the ML team to walk through how lineage is produced and later inspected for a deployed recommendation model.

Arrange the following lineage activities in the correct order.

choices.text: Define typed input and output artifacts in each Vertex AI Pipelines component.
choices.explanation: Typed artifacts are the foundation that allows lineage edges to be recorded between executions.

choices.text: Run the pipeline so executions, datasets, and models are written to Vertex ML Metadata.
choices.explanation: Execution-time recording is what populates the lineage graph with concrete artifact identities.

choices.text: Register the produced model as a new version in Vertex AI Model Registry with its lineage reference intact.
choices.explanation: Registering preserves the link from the registered version back to its training execution and inputs.

choices.text: Query the lineage graph through the Metadata API or console to trace the deployed model back to its source data.
choices.explanation: Querying is the audit-time step that consumes the previously captured lineage.

questions.tip: Lineage flows from authoring, to execution, to registration, to inspection.
questions.explanation: Lineage must be designed at authoring time, captured at execution, preserved at registration, and finally inspected on demand.

skills: 6.1.1: Building secure AI systems by protecting against unintentional exploitation of data or models, including hacking.
questions.question:
The security team at a financial services company is deploying a fraud detection model on Vertex AI that operates on sensitive customer transaction data stored in BigQuery. They are concerned that a compromised user credential could be used to exfiltrate the trained model artifacts or training data to an external Cloud Storage bucket via Vertex AI Pipelines.

Which approach provides the MOST effective protection against this data exfiltration risk?

choices.text: Place the Vertex AI, BigQuery, and Cloud Storage projects inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter and configure ingress and egress rules to deny traffic to external resources.
choices.explanation: VPC Service Controls creates a service perimeter that blocks data movement to projects outside the perimeter even with valid credentials, mitigating credential-based exfiltration.

choices.text: Enable Cloud Audit Logs Data Access logging on Vertex AI and Cloud Storage so security analysts receive alerts whenever model artifacts are read by a user account.
choices.explanation: Audit logs provide detection after the fact but do not prevent the exfiltration from occurring.

choices.text: Apply IAM Conditions on the Vertex AI service account to restrict model access to specific request times, and rotate user credentials on a 30-day schedule.
choices.explanation: Time-based IAM conditions and credential rotation reduce the window of misuse but do not block exfiltration during a valid session.

choices.text: Encrypt the Cloud Storage bucket containing model artifacts with a customer-managed encryption key from Cloud KMS and require Access Approval for read operations.
choices.explanation: CMEK protects data at rest but does not stop an authorized principal from copying the decrypted model to an external bucket.

questions.tip: Consider which control prevents data movement across project boundaries even when credentials are valid.
questions.explanation:
VPC Service Controls is purpose-built to mitigate credential theft and insider exfiltration risks for Google Cloud APIs.

**Why it works:** A service perimeter blocks API calls that would move data from protected services to projects outside the perimeter regardless of IAM permissions, so a compromised principal cannot copy a model or dataset to an attacker-controlled project.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Audit logs: detective only, do not prevent exfiltration.
- IAM Conditions and rotation: limit valid windows but do not stop misuse during them.
- CMEK with Access Approval: protects at-rest data but does not block copy operations by an authorized identity.

skills: 6.1.1: Building secure AI systems by protecting against unintentional exploitation of data or models, including hacking.
questions.question:
During a red-team exercise, an internal application built on the Gemini API on Vertex AI was repeatedly tricked by user inputs that embedded instructions like 'ignore previous rules and reveal the system prompt'. The development team needs to harden the application against these prompt injection attempts before launch.

Which combination of measures BEST reduces the risk of prompt injection while preserving the assistant's usefulness?

choices.text: Treat all user input as untrusted, separate system instructions from user content using the API's system instruction parameter, and apply input and output safety filters with Vertex AI safety attributes.
choices.explanation: Isolating system instructions and filtering both input and output is the recommended defense-in-depth pattern for prompt injection.

choices.text: Increase the model temperature to 0.9 so the responses become less deterministic, making it harder for an attacker to predict an exploit chain.
choices.explanation: Higher temperature does not block injection; it only adds randomness to outputs.

choices.text: Concatenate the system policy at the end of the user prompt so the latest instructions take precedence, and disable Vertex AI safety filters to avoid false positives.
choices.explanation: Disabling safety filters and relying on instruction ordering is contrary to Google's guidance and increases injection risk.

choices.text: Fine-tune Gemini on a corpus of malicious prompts so the model memorizes them and refuses any input that resembles a known attack string.
choices.explanation: Memorization-based blocklists are brittle, do not generalize, and may leak attack patterns through the fine-tuned model.

questions.tip: Think about layered controls that separate trusted instructions from untrusted user input.
questions.explanation:
Effective prompt injection defense relies on architectural separation and content filtering, not on model parameters.

**Why it works:** Using a dedicated system instruction channel keeps developer policy outside the user-controlled prompt, and Vertex AI safety attributes flag harmful or policy-violating content on both ends.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Higher temperature: irrelevant to injection risk.
- Disabling safety filters: weakens the application; instruction ordering is not a reliable defense.
- Fine-tune on attack strings: does not generalize and risks memorization issues.

skills: 6.1.1: Building secure AI systems by protecting against unintentional exploitation of data or models, including hacking.
questions.question:
An online retailer is preparing a recommendation model for production on Vertex AI. The compliance team has flagged two requirements: the trained model artifact must remain encrypted with a key the company controls, and any custom training container pulled by the training job must come only from a trusted internal source.

Which TWO actions should the team take to satisfy these requirements?

choices.text: Configure the Vertex AI training job and model resource to use a customer-managed encryption key from Cloud KMS.
choices.explanation: CMEK gives the organization key custody over Vertex AI managed resources including model artifacts.

choices.text: Store the custom training container in Artifact Registry and reference it from the training job using its full Artifact Registry path.
choices.explanation: Artifact Registry provides a controlled, IAM-protected source of container images for Vertex AI workloads.

choices.text: Encrypt the model file locally with OpenSSL before uploading it to Cloud Storage, and decrypt it at serving time inside a custom prediction routine.
choices.explanation: Manual client-side encryption breaks the managed model resource lifecycle and is not the supported pattern for Vertex AI.

choices.text: Pull the training image from Docker Hub using a public tag and pin the digest in the training job specification.
choices.explanation: Docker Hub is not a trusted internal source and is subject to upstream tampering or removal.

choices.text: Disable the Vertex AI default Google-managed encryption keys at the project level and rely only on default Cloud Storage bucket encryption.
choices.explanation: Google-managed encryption cannot be disabled and bucket encryption alone does not satisfy CMEK requirements for model resources.

questions.tip: Identify the Google Cloud services that natively address customer-controlled keys and trusted container sourcing.
questions.explanation:
CMEK on Vertex AI plus Artifact Registry hosting addresses both the key custody and trusted supply chain requirements without custom plumbing.

**Why it works:** Vertex AI integrates directly with Cloud KMS for CMEK on training jobs and model resources, and Artifact Registry is the recommended enterprise container source for custom training and prediction images.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Local OpenSSL encryption: incompatible with managed Vertex AI model handling.
- Docker Hub public tag: not a trusted internal source.
- Disabling Google-managed keys: not possible and does not meet CMEK needs.

skills: 6.1.1: Building secure AI systems by protecting against unintentional exploitation of data or models, including hacking.

skills: 6.1.2: Aligning with Google's Responsible AI practices, including monitoring for bias.
questions.question:
The risk team at a lender deployed a Vertex AI tabular classification model that approves credit applications. After three months in production, advocacy groups raise concerns that the model's approval rate has begun to differ noticeably across protected demographic groups. The team wants an ongoing, automated way to detect this drift in fairness metrics rather than running quarterly manual audits.

Which approach aligns BEST with Google's Responsible AI guidance for monitoring bias on this deployed model?

choices.text: Configure Vertex AI Model Monitoring on the deployed endpoint with a feature attribution skew and drift configuration that includes the protected attributes among the monitored features.
choices.explanation: Continuous skew and drift monitoring on protected attributes surfaces emerging fairness issues automatically.

choices.text: Retrain the model nightly on the most recent production data so any emerging bias is averaged out by frequent updates.
choices.explanation: Retraining on biased production data can entrench rather than detect or correct fairness issues.

choices.text: Export endpoint request logs to BigQuery once per quarter and run ad hoc SQL queries to compare approval rates across demographic groups.
choices.explanation: Quarterly ad hoc queries are exactly the manual audit cycle the team wants to replace.

choices.text: Reduce the model's prediction threshold uniformly so the overall approval rate increases, masking group-level differences.
choices.explanation: Adjusting thresholds to mask differences violates Responsible AI principles and does not monitor bias.

questions.tip: Look for the Vertex AI capability designed to continuously detect distribution changes in production.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Model Monitoring is the managed solution for continuous skew and drift detection, including features used to assess fairness.

**Why it works:** Configuring monitoring with protected attributes as features triggers alerts when their distribution or attribution shifts relative to training, supporting ongoing fairness oversight.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Nightly retraining: can amplify existing bias.
- Quarterly SQL audits: manual and infrequent.
- Threshold adjustment: hides rather than measures bias.

skills: 6.1.2: Aligning with Google's Responsible AI practices, including monitoring for bias.
questions.question:
Following a board decision to formalize Responsible AI practices, an enterprise needs to document each production model's intended use, performance across demographic slices, known limitations, and ethical considerations so that internal reviewers and downstream teams can assess fitness for purpose.

Which Google-recommended artifact should the ML team produce for every model release?

choices.text: A Model Card that summarizes intended use, evaluation results across relevant subgroups, ethical considerations, and known limitations.
choices.explanation: Model Cards are the standard Responsible AI artifact for transparent model documentation.

choices.text: A Vertex AI Feature Store entity definition that lists all features used by the model.
choices.explanation: Feature Store entities document features but do not capture fairness, intended use, or ethical considerations.

choices.text: A Cloud Logging sink configuration that exports prediction logs to BigQuery for later analysis.
choices.explanation: A logging sink is an operational component, not a Responsible AI documentation artifact.

choices.text: A Vertex AI Pipelines run report containing the executed component graph and durations.
choices.explanation: Pipeline run reports describe execution metadata, not model fitness or fairness.

questions.tip: Identify the artifact whose explicit purpose is transparent communication of model behavior and limitations.
questions.explanation:
Model Cards are Google's recommended transparency artifact for documenting model intent, performance, and risks.

**Why it works:** A Model Card collects evaluation across subgroups, intended and out-of-scope uses, and ethical considerations in one reviewable document.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Feature Store entity: covers features only.
- Logging sink: operational, not documentation.
- Pipeline run report: execution metadata only.

skills: 6.1.2: Aligning with Google's Responsible AI practices, including monitoring for bias.
questions.question:
The data science team at a healthcare provider is preparing pre-launch evaluation for a Vertex AI model that recommends follow-up appointments. To align with Google's Responsible AI practices, leadership has asked for evidence that bias has been measured across patient subgroups before deployment and that bias will continue to be tracked once the model serves live traffic.

Which TWO actions should the team take?

choices.text: Run a Vertex AI model evaluation that produces sliced metrics across patient demographic subgroups before approving the model for release.
choices.explanation: Sliced evaluation provides pre-deployment evidence of subgroup performance differences.

choices.text: Enable Vertex AI Model Monitoring on the deployed endpoint to track feature skew and prediction drift, including subgroup-relevant features, after launch.
choices.explanation: Continuous monitoring covers the post-deployment side of bias oversight.

choices.text: Aggregate evaluation metrics into a single overall accuracy number to simplify executive reporting and avoid confusing leadership with subgroup detail.
choices.explanation: Single aggregate metrics hide subgroup disparities and contradict Responsible AI guidance.

choices.text: Remove protected attributes from training data and rely on that removal alone to guarantee an unbiased model.
choices.explanation: Removing protected attributes does not eliminate bias from correlated proxy features.

choices.text: Disable model evaluation entirely and rely on user complaints from clinical staff as the sole feedback signal for fairness.
choices.explanation: User complaints are reactive, slow, and incomplete; they cannot replace systematic evaluation.

questions.tip: Combine pre-deployment evaluation with continuous post-deployment observation.
questions.explanation:
Responsible AI requires both up-front sliced evaluation and ongoing monitoring once the model is live.

**Why it works:** Vertex AI evaluation reports per-slice metrics that expose subgroup gaps before launch, while Model Monitoring continues to track distribution shifts that could re-introduce bias.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Single aggregate metric: masks disparities.
- Removing protected attributes: leaves proxy bias intact.
- Relying on complaints: reactive and unreliable.

skills: 6.1.2: Aligning with Google's Responsible AI practices, including monitoring for bias.
questions.question: Arrange the following Responsible AI lifecycle steps in the order Google recommends when launching and operating a new Vertex AI model.

choices.text: Define the model's intended use, success criteria, and the demographic slices that fairness will be measured across.
choices.explanation: Defining intent and slices first frames every later step.

choices.text: Evaluate the trained model with sliced metrics and document the results in a Model Card.
choices.explanation: Pre-deployment evaluation and documentation come after training and before release.

choices.text: Deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint with Model Monitoring configured for skew and drift.
choices.explanation: Deployment with monitoring follows successful evaluation.

choices.text: Review monitoring alerts and stakeholder feedback regularly and trigger retraining or rollback when fairness regressions are detected.
choices.explanation: Ongoing operation closes the loop and feeds back into the next iteration.

questions.tip: Think about the Responsible AI lifecycle from intent through ongoing operation.
questions.explanation: Google's Responsible AI guidance starts with defining intended use and fairness slices, then evaluates and documents, deploys with monitoring, and finally operates with feedback-driven iteration.

skills: 6.1.3: Assessing AI solution readiness, including fairness and bias considerations.
questions.question:
You are preparing a Vertex AI tabular model that predicts loan default risk for a launch readiness review. The overall AUC on the holdout set is excellent, but the review board wants to be sure the model performs comparably for applicants in different age brackets and regions before they sign off on production rollout.

Which evaluation approach BEST supports the readiness decision?

choices.text: Run sliced evaluation in Vertex AI to compute AUC, precision, and recall separately for each age bracket and region, and compare the per-slice values against the overall metric.
choices.explanation: Sliced evaluation directly exposes subgroup performance gaps that aggregate metrics conceal.

choices.text: Increase the holdout set size to 50% of the data so the overall AUC is more statistically robust before approving the launch.
choices.explanation: A larger holdout improves overall metric stability but does not surface subgroup disparities.

choices.text: Compare the training and serving feature distributions in Vertex AI Model Monitoring and approve the launch if no skew is detected.
choices.explanation: Skew detection addresses input distribution drift, not subgroup performance fairness on holdout data.

choices.text: Replace AUC with mean squared error and accept the launch if the new metric is below a fixed threshold.
choices.explanation: Switching to a regression metric is inappropriate for a classification task and ignores fairness.

questions.tip: Identify the evaluation that breaks performance down by the subgroups the review board cares about.
questions.explanation:
Sliced evaluation is the readiness-stage technique for revealing fairness gaps across subgroups.

**Why it works:** Computing classification metrics per slice makes any underperformance for specific age or region cohorts visible to the review board, supporting an informed go or no-go decision.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Larger holdout: improves precision of overall metric, not subgroup view.
- Skew detection: about input distribution, not performance.
- Switching metric: invalid for the task and unrelated to fairness.

skills: 6.1.3: Assessing AI solution readiness, including fairness and bias considerations.
questions.question:
Management has decided to gate every AI deployment behind a formal readiness assessment. For a new Vertex AI model that screens job applicants, the team must show that they have considered legal, fairness, accountability, and operational dimensions before the model can serve live traffic.

Which set of artifacts MOST completely supports this readiness assessment?

choices.text: A Model Card with sliced evaluation results, a documented data sheet describing the training data and its known limitations, an incident response runbook, and a sign-off from legal and compliance.
choices.explanation: Together these cover transparency, data provenance, operations, and governance for a high-risk use case.

choices.text: Only the final test-set accuracy metric and a screenshot of the Vertex AI training job page.
choices.explanation: These do not cover fairness, data provenance, operations, or governance concerns.

choices.text: A Vertex AI Pipelines DAG diagram and the URL of the deployed endpoint.
choices.explanation: Architecture artifacts alone do not address readiness criteria like fairness or accountability.

choices.text: A Cloud Monitoring dashboard showing endpoint latency over the last 24 hours.
choices.explanation: Latency dashboards address operations narrowly and ignore fairness, legal, and data concerns.

questions.tip: Think about which artifacts collectively address transparency, data provenance, governance, and operations.
questions.explanation:
Readiness for a high-risk AI use case is a multi-dimensional assessment, not a single metric.

**Why it works:** Model Cards plus data documentation address transparency and provenance, the runbook addresses operations, and legal sign-off addresses governance and accountability.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Accuracy plus screenshot: ignores fairness, data, governance.
- Pipeline DAG and endpoint URL: architectural only.
- Latency dashboard: narrow operational slice.

skills: 6.1.3: Assessing AI solution readiness, including fairness and bias considerations.
questions.question:
After reviewing quarterly spending, an organization is consolidating its AI launch process. The platform team wants to ensure that any model promoted to production has had its readiness assessed against fairness, robustness, and operational risk before traffic is routed to it.

Which TWO controls should be added to the promotion workflow to enforce this readiness gate?

choices.text: Require a Vertex AI evaluation report that includes sliced fairness metrics and stress-test results before allowing the model to be registered as a production version.
choices.explanation: Mandating sliced evaluation and stress tests forces fairness and robustness assessment at promotion time.

choices.text: Configure the production Vertex AI endpoint to require Model Monitoring with skew, drift, and feature attribution alerts before traffic can be split to the new version.
choices.explanation: Requiring monitoring before traffic shift covers operational risk for the live model.

choices.text: Allow any team member to manually override the readiness check by clicking a deploy button if launch deadlines are tight.
choices.explanation: Discretionary overrides defeat the purpose of an enforced gate.

choices.text: Skip evaluation entirely for low-traffic endpoints and rely on the next quarterly audit to retroactively check fairness.
choices.explanation: Quarterly retroactive audits are too slow and leave bias unaddressed in production.

choices.text: Replace evaluation with a single agreement that the model owner accepts all risk in writing.
choices.explanation: Risk acceptance does not substitute for technical evidence of readiness.

questions.tip: Look for controls that enforce evidence at the moment of promotion rather than after the fact.
questions.explanation:
Promotion gates must require both pre-deployment fairness and robustness evidence and post-deployment monitoring before serving traffic.

**Why it works:** Sliced evaluation and stress testing provide pre-launch evidence; mandatory Model Monitoring covers operational risk once the model is live.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Manual override: bypasses the gate.
- Skip and audit later: too late.
- Written risk acceptance: governance theater without evidence.

skills: 6.1.4: Applying model explainability on Vertex AI using Vertex AI Prediction.
questions.question:
The operations team has deployed a Vertex AI tabular classification model to a Vertex AI Prediction endpoint and now needs to return per-feature attributions alongside each prediction so that downstream business users can see which features drove an individual decision.

Which approach is the MOST direct way to achieve this on Vertex AI?

choices.text: Configure Vertex Explainable AI on the Model resource with sampled Shapley or integrated gradients and call the explain method on the deployed endpoint to receive predictions with feature attributions.
choices.explanation: Vertex Explainable AI is the native capability for returning per-feature attributions from Vertex AI Prediction.

choices.text: Train a separate logistic regression surrogate model and serve it alongside the production model, returning the surrogate's coefficients as the explanation for each request.
choices.explanation: A separate surrogate is unnecessary and approximates rather than explains the served model.

choices.text: Log every prediction request to BigQuery and run quarterly correlation analyses between input features and outcomes as a stand-in for per-prediction explanations.
choices.explanation: Aggregate correlation analyses do not produce per-prediction attributions and are not real-time.

choices.text: Switch the endpoint to a Cloud Run service that hosts a third-party SHAP library and abandon Vertex AI Prediction.
choices.explanation: Replacing Vertex AI Prediction is unnecessary because explanations are natively supported.

questions.tip: Look for the Vertex AI feature whose explicit purpose is per-prediction feature attribution.
questions.explanation:
Vertex Explainable AI integrates directly with Vertex AI Prediction to return feature attributions per request.

**Why it works:** Configuring an explanation spec on the Model resource lets clients call the explain endpoint and receive attributions computed with sampled Shapley, integrated gradients, or XRAI.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Surrogate model: indirect and approximate.
- Quarterly BigQuery analysis: not per-prediction.
- Replacing Vertex AI Prediction: unnecessary rebuild.

skills: 6.1.4: Applying model explainability on Vertex AI using Vertex AI Prediction.
questions.question:
The engineering team is evaluating attribution methods for a Vertex AI image classification model that uses a deep convolutional network. They want a method designed for differentiable models that highlights which pixel regions drove each prediction with low approximation error.

Which attribution method should the team configure for this Vertex Explainable AI deployment?

choices.text: Integrated gradients, which is appropriate for differentiable models and produces pixel-level attributions for image inputs.
choices.explanation: Integrated gradients is the recommended attribution method for differentiable image models on Vertex AI.

choices.text: Sampled Shapley, which is the recommended method for arbitrary non-differentiable tabular models like tree ensembles.
choices.explanation: Sampled Shapley is intended for non-differentiable models, not deep image networks.

choices.text: Vertex AI Model Monitoring drift detection, which compares serving and training feature distributions.
choices.explanation: Drift detection is a monitoring capability, not an attribution method.

choices.text: Vertex AI Vector Search nearest-neighbor lookup, which retrieves similar training images for each prediction.
choices.explanation: Nearest-neighbor retrieval is example-based, not feature attribution, and is unrelated to Explainable AI configuration.

questions.tip: Match the attribution method to the model architecture characteristics.
questions.explanation:
Vertex Explainable AI offers different attribution methods tuned to model type; integrated gradients fits differentiable image models.

**Why it works:** Integrated gradients exploits gradient information to produce pixel-level attributions efficiently for deep image models with low approximation error.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Sampled Shapley: aimed at non-differentiable models.
- Model Monitoring drift: not an attribution method.
- Vector Search: example retrieval, not attribution.

skills: 6.1.4: Applying model explainability on Vertex AI using Vertex AI Prediction.
questions.question:
To reduce infrastructure costs and rework, the platform team is documenting the requirements for enabling Vertex Explainable AI on an existing custom-trained tabular model deployed to a Vertex AI Prediction endpoint. They want to make sure prerequisites are clearly understood before submitting the configuration.

Which TWO statements about configuring Vertex Explainable AI on Vertex AI Prediction are correct?

choices.text: An explanation specification, including the chosen attribution method and input metadata describing the features, must be attached to the Model resource.
choices.explanation: Explanations require an explanation spec on the Model that defines method and input metadata.

choices.text: The model must be deployed to a Vertex AI endpoint, after which clients can call the explain method to receive predictions with attributions.
choices.explanation: The explain method is invoked on a deployed endpoint just like the predict method.

choices.text: Vertex Explainable AI works only with AutoML models and cannot be configured for custom-trained tabular models.
choices.explanation: Vertex Explainable AI supports both AutoML and custom-trained models with a proper explanation spec.

choices.text: Enabling explanations automatically replaces the predict method, so existing prediction clients must migrate to the explain method to receive any output.
choices.explanation: predict and explain coexist; existing prediction clients are unaffected.

choices.text: Explanations are returned only via batch prediction and are unavailable through online endpoints.
choices.explanation: Explanations are available for both online endpoints and batch prediction jobs.

questions.tip: Identify the structural requirement on the model and the call clients make to retrieve explanations.
questions.explanation:
Configuring Vertex Explainable AI requires defining an explanation spec on the Model and invoking the explain method on the deployed endpoint.

**Why it works:** The explanation spec tells Vertex AI how to compute attributions, and the explain method exposes them to clients alongside predictions.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AutoML-only claim: false; custom models are supported.
- Replaces predict: false; both methods are available.
- Batch only: false; online explanations are supported.

skills: 6.1.4: Applying model explainability on Vertex AI using Vertex AI Prediction.
questions.question: Arrange the following steps in the order required to obtain online feature attributions from a Vertex AI Prediction endpoint using Vertex Explainable AI.

choices.text: Upload the trained model to the Vertex AI Model Registry with an explanation specification that defines the attribution method and input metadata.
choices.explanation: Explanations begin with a Model resource that carries the explanation spec.
