skills: 6.2.1: Establishing continuous evaluation metrics using Vertex AI Model Monitoring and Explainable AI.
questions.question:
The data science team at a retail analytics firm has deployed a tabular customer-churn model to a Vertex AI endpoint that receives roughly 50,000 prediction requests per day. They want a managed signal that automatically flags when the statistical properties of incoming features start drifting away from the original training data so that retraining can be triggered before churn predictions degrade.

Which Vertex AI Model Monitoring configuration MOST directly addresses this requirement?

choices.text: Enable a training-serving skew detection job on the endpoint, supply the original training dataset as the baseline, and configure per-feature alerting thresholds with email notifications.
choices.explanation: Skew detection compares production input distributions against the supplied training baseline and alerts when distributions diverge beyond the configured threshold.

choices.text: Enable prediction drift detection on the endpoint, leave the training dataset unset, and configure thresholds against the most recent 24 hours of predictions.
choices.explanation: Drift detection compares recent production data against an earlier production window, not against the training dataset, so it cannot detect divergence from the original training distribution.

choices.text: Schedule a Vertex AI Pipelines job that runs the model evaluation component daily on a held-out test set and writes results to BigQuery.
choices.explanation: Evaluating against a static test set measures offline accuracy but does not track distribution changes in live serving traffic.

choices.text: Configure Cloud Logging metric-based alerts on the endpoint's prediction latency and error count.
choices.explanation: Latency and error metrics describe operational health, not feature distribution shift, so they would not flag input data quality issues.

questions.tip: Distinguish between comparing live data to a training baseline versus comparing live data to itself over time.
questions.explanation:
Continuous evaluation against the original training distribution is the role of training-serving skew detection in Vertex AI Model Monitoring.

**Why it works:** Skew jobs ingest the training dataset as the reference and compute statistical distance metrics (such as L-infinity for categorical and Jensen-Shannon for numerical features) against sampled prediction inputs, raising alerts when thresholds are crossed.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Drift detection: uses a recent production baseline, not the training dataset.
- Scheduled evaluation pipeline: measures offline accuracy, not input distribution shift.
- Logging alerts: track operational signals, not feature statistics.

skills: 6.2.1: Establishing continuous evaluation metrics using Vertex AI Model Monitoring and Explainable AI.
questions.question:
During a quarterly model governance review, a regulated lender must continuously demonstrate which input features most influence each individual loan-approval prediction served from a custom-trained Vertex AI model. The compliance team requires that explanations be generated automatically alongside every online prediction without rebuilding the serving stack.

Which approach is the MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Upload the model to the Vertex AI Model Registry with an explanation specification (sampled Shapley) and deploy to an endpoint, then call the explain method on the endpoint for each prediction.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI Explainable AI supports per-instance feature attributions when a model is registered with an explanation spec and served on an endpoint.

choices.text: Train a separate surrogate logistic regression model offline and use its coefficients as a global proxy for feature importance during reviews.
choices.explanation: Global surrogate coefficients do not provide per-prediction attributions and may not faithfully represent the original model.

choices.text: Enable Vertex AI Model Monitoring with prediction drift detection and inspect the per-feature drift scores as a substitute for explanations.
choices.explanation: Drift scores describe distribution change over time, not the contribution of features to a specific prediction.

choices.text: Stream prediction requests to BigQuery and compute Pearson correlation between each feature and the prediction column on a daily schedule.
choices.explanation: Correlation analysis is an aggregate statistic and cannot attribute a specific decision to specific features for any single applicant.

questions.tip: Match the requirement (per-prediction attributions) to the capability that produces them natively.
questions.explanation:
Explainable AI on Vertex AI provides feature attributions per prediction when an explanation spec is attached at model upload.

**Why it works:** Methods such as sampled Shapley, integrated gradients, and XRAI compute the contribution of each input feature for the specific instance scored, satisfying per-decision auditability.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Surrogate model: gives only global, approximate insight.
- Drift detection: explains distribution shift, not predictions.
- Correlation in BigQuery: aggregate, not per-instance.

skills: 6.2.1: Establishing continuous evaluation metrics using Vertex AI Model Monitoring and Explainable AI.
questions.question:
The MLOps team is enabling a Vertex AI Model Monitoring job for a deployed tabular model and needs the job to produce continuous evaluation metrics that can later be reviewed in the Google Cloud console.

Which TWO configuration items must be supplied when creating the monitoring job?

choices.text: A sampling rate (or sample size) that controls what fraction of online prediction requests are logged for analysis.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI Model Monitoring requires you to define how prediction requests are sampled before statistics can be computed.

choices.text: A monitoring frequency that defines how often the analysis runs over the collected prediction window.
choices.explanation: The job needs an analysis cadence to bucket logged predictions and emit metrics on a recurring schedule.

choices.text: A Cloud Armor security policy attached to the endpoint to filter monitored traffic.
choices.explanation: Cloud Armor protects HTTP(S) load balancers and is unrelated to model monitoring configuration.

choices.text: A Dataflow template name to materialize each batch of predictions into a Cloud SQL instance.
choices.explanation: Model Monitoring uses managed sampling and analysis; users do not provide a Dataflow template.

choices.text: A Pub/Sub topic that the job uses to receive ground-truth labels in real time.
choices.explanation: Real-time label ingestion through Pub/Sub is not a required input; skew and drift jobs operate on feature distributions, not labels.

questions.tip: Think about what the job needs in order to collect data and decide when to compute statistics.
questions.explanation:
A Model Monitoring job needs both an input sampling configuration and an analysis schedule.

**Why it works:** Sampling controls what proportion of live traffic is captured to a request-response log, and the monitoring frequency drives the recurring statistical analysis that produces metrics.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cloud Armor: a network security control, not a monitoring input.
- Dataflow template: not part of Model Monitoring's managed pipeline.
- Pub/Sub for labels: skew and drift jobs work on inputs, not labels.

skills: 6.2.1: Establishing continuous evaluation metrics using Vertex AI Model Monitoring and Explainable AI.
questions.question:
An MLOps engineer is establishing continuous evaluation for a newly trained classification model. The model will be served online with both feature attributions and skew monitoring enabled.

Arrange the following deployment steps in the correct order.

choices.text: Upload the trained model to the Vertex AI Model Registry, attaching an explanation specification.
choices.explanation: The model artifact and its explanation metadata must exist in the registry before a deployable version can be created.

choices.text: Deploy the model version to a Vertex AI endpoint with traffic split configured.
choices.explanation: An endpoint is required to receive online predictions and to be the target of monitoring.

choices.text: Create a Model Monitoring job on the endpoint that references the original training dataset as the skew baseline.
choices.explanation: Monitoring is configured against an existing endpoint and needs the training data as its baseline.

choices.text: Review feature attribution and skew metrics in the console after sufficient prediction traffic has been logged.
choices.explanation: Metrics only appear once the job has analyzed a window of sampled predictions.

questions.tip: Consider what artifact each subsequent step depends on.
questions.explanation: Continuous evaluation requires the model and explanations registered, an endpoint deployed, monitoring attached to that endpoint, and finally the analysis output reviewed once data has accumulated.

skills: 6.2.2: Monitoring for training-serving skew.
questions.question:
The operations team at an insurance startup notices that a fraud-detection model deployed on a Vertex AI endpoint has begun rejecting an unusually high percentage of valid claims. They suspect that the live feature distributions no longer match what the model was trained on and want to confirm this with a managed comparison rather than ad-hoc analysis.

Which Vertex AI Model Monitoring capability is the MOST appropriate to enable?

choices.text: Training-serving skew detection, configured with the BigQuery URI of the original training dataset as the baseline and statistical thresholds set per feature.
choices.explanation: Skew detection is purpose-built to compare live request features against the training dataset distribution.

choices.text: Prediction drift detection without supplying any baseline dataset, allowing the service to infer one from the most recent hour of predictions.
choices.explanation: Drift detection compares newer production windows against earlier production windows, not against training data, so it cannot diagnose training-serving mismatch.

choices.text: A Cloud Monitoring uptime check that pings the prediction endpoint every minute and alerts on HTTP 5xx responses.
choices.explanation: Uptime checks measure availability, not feature distribution differences.

choices.text: Vertex AI Vizier study that explores hyperparameter ranges to suggest retraining configurations.
choices.explanation: Vizier optimizes hyperparameters; it does not detect distributional skew between training and serving data.

questions.tip: Match the comparison the team needs (training vs serving) to the feature designed for it.
questions.explanation:
Skew detection within Vertex AI Model Monitoring directly compares serving inputs against the original training distribution.

**Why it works:** When provided a training dataset URI, the monitoring job samples online predictions and computes per-feature distance metrics against the training reference, alerting when thresholds are exceeded.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Drift without baseline: only compares production to itself.
- Uptime check: measures availability, not data quality.
- Vizier: a hyperparameter tuning service.

skills: 6.2.2: Monitoring for training-serving skew.
questions.question:
Following a board decision to formalize ML governance, the platform team must enable training-serving skew monitoring for a custom-trained tabular model. Their training data lives in a partitioned BigQuery table and they need the monitoring job to use it as the reference distribution.

What is the MOST appropriate way to point the skew job at this baseline?

choices.text: Provide the BigQuery table URI in the training dataset configuration and specify the target (label) column so feature statistics can be computed automatically.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI Model Monitoring accepts BigQuery (and Cloud Storage) datasets as the training baseline and computes feature statistics on your behalf.

choices.text: Manually pre-compute summary statistics in a notebook and paste them into the monitoring job's threshold fields one feature at a time.
choices.explanation: The service computes baseline statistics from the supplied dataset; manual entry of distributions is not the supported path.

choices.text: Export the BigQuery table to Cloud SQL and configure a JDBC connection on the monitoring job.
choices.explanation: Model Monitoring does not accept Cloud SQL as a baseline source.

choices.text: Stream the training data through Pub/Sub into the monitoring job in real time.
choices.explanation: Skew baselines are static datasets, not streaming sources.

questions.tip: Recall which storage sources Vertex AI Model Monitoring natively reads as a training baseline.
questions.explanation:
Skew monitoring jobs accept the training data location directly as a BigQuery URI or Cloud Storage path.

**Why it works:** The service computes baseline feature statistics from the referenced dataset, eliminating manual pre-computation and ensuring per-feature thresholds are evaluated against authoritative training data.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Manual statistics: not how the API is configured.
- Cloud SQL export: not a supported baseline source.
- Streaming through Pub/Sub: baselines are static.

skills: 6.2.2: Monitoring for training-serving skew.
questions.question:
The engineering team is reviewing alert thresholds for a training-serving skew monitoring job on a Vertex AI endpoint. They want each per-feature alert to fire only when the statistical difference between training and serving distributions is meaningfully large, while keeping the configuration aligned with the metric Vertex AI uses by default.

Which TWO statements are correct about the default skew metrics and thresholds?

choices.text: L-infinity distance is used by default to compare distributions of categorical features between training and serving data.
choices.explanation: Categorical feature skew is measured with L-infinity (the maximum absolute difference between category probabilities) by default.

choices.text: Jensen-Shannon divergence is used by default to compare distributions of numerical features between training and serving data.
choices.explanation: Numerical feature skew uses Jensen-Shannon divergence by default to compare bucketed distributions.

choices.text: A single global threshold is applied to all features and cannot be adjusted per feature.
choices.explanation: Thresholds can be configured globally and per individual feature.

choices.text: Skew thresholds are evaluated against label drift rather than against feature distributions.
choices.explanation: Skew analysis compares feature distributions; label-based comparisons are a separate concern.

choices.text: Skew jobs require ground-truth labels to be supplied for every prediction in real time.
choices.explanation: Skew detection works on input feature distributions and does not need real-time labels.

questions.tip: Recall which default distance metric is used for each feature type.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Model Monitoring uses L-infinity for categorical features and Jensen-Shannon divergence for numerical features when computing skew.

**Why it works:** These metrics quantify the gap between training and serving probability distributions in a way that is appropriate for each data type.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Global-only thresholds: per-feature thresholds are supported.
- Label drift: skew evaluates input features.
- Real-time labels: not required for skew jobs.

skills: 6.2.2: Monitoring for training-serving skew.

Choosing how often statistics are computed on live traffic

Receiving notifications when a feature crosses its allowed deviation

choices.text: Training dataset URI supplied to the monitoring job
choices.explanation: Defines the baseline distribution for skew comparison.

choices.text: Prediction request sampling rate
choices.explanation: Determines what fraction of online requests are logged.

choices.text: Monitoring analysis frequency
choices.explanation: Sets the interval for recomputing distribution statistics.

choices.text: Email alerting threshold per feature
choices.explanation: Triggers notifications when distance metrics exceed limits.

questions.tip: Map each operational question to the specific job parameter that controls it.
questions.explanation: A complete skew monitoring setup combines a baseline source, a sampling rate, an analysis cadence, and per-feature alerting thresholds.

skills: 6.2.3: Monitoring for feature attribution drift.
questions.question:
The data science team at a logistics provider has deployed a delivery-ETA model on Vertex AI. They want an automated signal that fires when the relative importance of input features in production drifts away from what it was at training time, even when raw feature distributions look similar.

Which monitoring approach is the MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Enable Vertex AI Model Monitoring with feature attribution drift detection, configured against the training dataset baseline so attributions are compared over time.
choices.explanation: Feature attribution drift detection uses Explainable AI attributions and compares their distribution over time against a baseline.

choices.text: Enable training-serving skew detection on the raw input features only, without enabling Explainable AI on the model.
choices.explanation: Raw feature skew can miss shifts in how features influence predictions; attribution-based monitoring is required for that signal.

choices.text: Schedule a Cloud Scheduler job that retrains the model every week regardless of monitoring signals.
choices.explanation: Scheduled retraining is not a detection mechanism and ignores whether attributions have actually changed.

choices.text: Use BigQuery ML to compute a Pearson correlation between each feature column and the prediction column on a daily basis.
choices.explanation: Correlation does not capture attribution magnitudes from the deployed model and conflates association with feature importance.

questions.tip: Look for the option that explicitly compares model-derived feature importance over time.
questions.explanation:
Feature attribution drift detection uses Explainable AI attributions to track shifts in feature importance over time.

**Why it works:** The job computes attributions on sampled production predictions and compares their average magnitude per feature against the training baseline, alerting when attribution patterns shift even if input distributions look stable.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Raw skew only: ignores changes in feature influence.
- Scheduled retraining: not a monitoring signal.
- Pearson correlation: not a faithful proxy for attributions.

skills: 6.2.3: Monitoring for feature attribution drift.
questions.question:
The MLOps team is preparing to enable feature attribution drift monitoring on a deployed Vertex AI model and discovers the monitoring job creation fails with an error indicating that explanations are not configured.

What is the MOST likely cause and resolution?

choices.text: The model was uploaded to the Vertex AI Model Registry without an explanation specification; re-upload the model with an explanation spec attached and redeploy before enabling attribution drift.
choices.explanation: Attribution drift requires the deployed model to support explanations, which requires an explanation spec at upload time.

choices.text: The endpoint is missing a Cloud Armor policy; attach a policy and re-create the monitoring job.
choices.explanation: Cloud Armor is unrelated to Explainable AI configuration.

choices.text: Object versioning must be enabled on the Cloud Storage bucket holding training artifacts before attribution drift can be computed.
choices.explanation: Bucket versioning has no bearing on whether explanations are available for a deployed model.

choices.text: The model needs to be exported to TensorFlow Lite format before attributions can be computed online.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI computes attributions on supported model formats served on endpoints; TFLite export is not required.

questions.tip: Attribution drift depends on the deployed model being able to produce explanations.
questions.explanation:
Feature attribution drift can only be computed when the deployed model has explanations enabled via an explanation specification.

**Why it works:** Without an explanation spec, the endpoint cannot return attributions, so the monitoring job has nothing to compare against the baseline. Re-uploading the model with the spec and redeploying restores the missing capability.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cloud Armor policy: a network control, not an explanations prerequisite.
- Bucket versioning: irrelevant.
- TFLite export: not a serving requirement.

skills: 6.2.3: Monitoring for feature attribution drift.
questions.question:
After reviewing quarterly spending, the platform team is rolling out feature attribution drift monitoring across several deployed Vertex AI models. They want to ensure their setup actually detects meaningful changes in feature importance over time without generating noisy alerts.

Which TWO actions BEST support this goal?

choices.text: Configure the monitoring job to use the original training dataset as the attribution baseline so production attributions are compared against a stable reference.
choices.explanation: A stable training baseline anchors comparisons so noise in production windows does not constantly redefine the reference.

choices.text: Set per-feature attribution drift thresholds that reflect the relative importance of each feature rather than a single global value.
choices.explanation: Tailored thresholds reduce false positives on low-impact features while keeping sensitivity on high-impact ones.

choices.text: Disable Explainable AI on the model to reduce the cost of computing attributions during monitoring.
choices.explanation: Disabling explanations would prevent attribution drift from being computed at all.

choices.text: Apply the same global threshold to all features regardless of their training importance.
choices.explanation: A single global threshold is a blunt instrument and tends to over- or under-alert depending on the feature.

choices.text: Replace attribution drift with prediction latency monitoring as a substitute for tracking feature influence.
choices.explanation: Latency does not reflect changes in feature importance.

questions.tip: Look for choices that combine a meaningful baseline with thoughtful threshold design.
questions.explanation:
A reliable attribution drift setup pairs a stable training baseline with feature-specific thresholds.

**Why it works:** The baseline gives the comparison anchoring, while per-feature thresholds match alert sensitivity to each feature's importance.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disabling Explainable AI: removes the data needed to detect drift.
- Global threshold only: noisy and inflexible.
- Latency monitoring: unrelated to feature influence.

skills: 6.2.4: Monitoring model performance against baselines, simpler models, and across the time dimension.
questions.question:
The engineering team is evaluating a new gradient-boosted model that is intended to replace a long-running logistic regression baseline for credit-risk scoring. Leadership wants ongoing assurance that the new model continues to outperform the baseline on identical holdout data over time.

Which approach is the MOST appropriate for sustained comparison?

choices.text: Run a recurring Vertex AI Pipelines job that uses the model evaluation component to score both models on the same holdout dataset and writes side-by-side metrics to BigQuery for trend dashboards.
choices.explanation: A scheduled evaluation pipeline computing identical metrics on both models against the same holdout supports apples-to-apples longitudinal comparison.

choices.text: Compare the training-time metrics of each model recorded in their respective Vertex AI Experiments runs and assume those values still hold in production.
choices.explanation: Training-time metrics are point-in-time and do not reflect ongoing performance against fresh data.

choices.text: Configure Vertex AI Model Monitoring skew detection on the new model only and infer relative performance from the alert rate.
choices.explanation: Skew detection measures input distribution shift, not comparative model accuracy.

choices.text: Manually run notebooks at the end of each quarter to compare metrics, with no scheduled cadence.
choices.explanation: Ad-hoc evaluation does not provide the continuous, repeatable comparison the requirement calls for.

questions.tip: Continuous, comparable measurement requires both repetition and consistent data.
questions.explanation:
A scheduled evaluation pipeline scoring both models on the same holdout is the cleanest route to longitudinal comparison.

**Why it works:** Vertex AI Pipelines orchestrates repeated runs of the model evaluation component, persists results to BigQuery, and yields a trend you can visualize.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Training-time metrics: not reflective of current performance.
- Skew detection: input-only signal.
- Manual quarterly notebooks: not continuous.

skills: 6.2.4: Monitoring model performance against baselines, simpler models, and across the time dimension.
questions.question:
Following a board decision to standardize ML reporting, a team needs to track and compare evaluation metrics across many candidate model versions, including a simple linear baseline, over the course of several months.

Which Google Cloud capability provides the MOST appropriate native experience for this?

choices.text: Use Vertex AI Experiments to log parameters, metrics, and artifacts for each run and compare runs side by side in the Vertex AI console.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI Experiments is designed to record and compare model training and evaluation runs across versions.

choices.text: Manually maintain a shared Google Sheet with metric values copy-pasted from training logs.
choices.explanation: Manual spreadsheets are error prone and lack lineage with the underlying model artifacts.

choices.text: Stream training logs to Cloud Logging and rely on free-text log search to compare metrics.
choices.explanation: Cloud Logging is a logs platform; it does not provide structured run comparison or visualization tailored to ML metrics.

choices.text: Save each run's metrics as a Pub/Sub message and rely on the topic backlog as the comparison record.
choices.explanation: Pub/Sub is a messaging service and is not a metrics tracking system.

questions.tip: Pick the service explicitly built for tracking and comparing ML runs.
questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Experiments natively records and compares parameters, metrics, and artifacts across model runs.

**Why it works:** Each run is logged with structured metadata, enabling side-by-side comparison and longitudinal tracking, including against a simple baseline run.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Spreadsheet: manual and lossy.
- Cloud Logging: not designed for ML run comparison.
- Pub/Sub: a transport mechanism, not a tracking system.

skills: 6.2.4: Monitoring model performance against baselines, simpler models, and across the time dimension.
questions.question:
Management has decided that every production model must be benchmarked monthly against a documented baseline as well as a simpler reference model, with metrics tracked across the time dimension.

Which TWO design choices BEST satisfy this policy?

choices.text: Persist each monthly evaluation result with a timestamp into a BigQuery table that is shared by all model evaluation runs.
choices.explanation: A timestamped, shared table provides a longitudinal record that supports trend analysis.

choices.text: Visualize the evolving metrics in Looker Studio dashboards built on the BigQuery evaluation table so stakeholders can see trends.
choices.explanation: Dashboards over the historical table directly satisfy the time-dimension visibility requirement.

choices.text: Overwrite the previous month's evaluation table to keep storage costs low.
choices.explanation: Overwriting destroys the longitudinal record needed for time-dimension monitoring.

choices.text: Compare models by visually inspecting confusion matrices saved as PNGs without storing numeric metrics.
choices.explanation: Image inspection is not scalable and does not produce machine-readable trend data.

choices.text: Replace the simple baseline with the production model itself once metrics start improving.
choices.explanation: Removing the baseline defeats the purpose of comparison and breaks longitudinal tracking.

questions.tip: Look for the pair that captures history and surfaces it for analysis.
questions.explanation:
Storing timestamped metrics in BigQuery and visualizing them in Looker Studio is the standard pattern for time-series ML performance monitoring on Google Cloud.

**Why it works:** Append-only tables preserve history, and dashboards turn that history into a continuous comparison view that includes the baseline and simpler model.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Overwriting: erases history.
- PNG inspection: not analyzable at scale.
- Removing the baseline: undermines comparison.

skills: 6.2.4: Monitoring model performance against baselines, simpler models, and across the time dimension.
questions.question:
The team is establishing a recurring benchmark that compares a candidate model against a simpler baseline on a fixed holdout set, with results tracked over time.

Arrange the following steps in the correct order.

choices.text: Curate and freeze a shared holdout dataset stored in BigQuery to act as the evaluation reference.
choices.explanation: A stable holdout must exist before any comparable scoring can take place.

choices.text: Score both the candidate model and the simpler baseline on the holdout using the Vertex AI model evaluation component.
choices.explanation: Both models need to be evaluated on the same dataset to produce comparable metrics.

choices.text: Append timestamped evaluation metrics for both models to a shared BigQuery results table.
choices.explanation: Persisting results creates the historical record used for time-dimension analysis.

choices.text: Review the evolving metrics in a Looker Studio dashboard during the monthly review meeting.
choices.explanation: Dashboards consume the accumulated history once enough runs exist.

questions.tip: Each step depends on the artifact produced by the one before.
questions.explanation: A frozen holdout, paired evaluation runs, persisted timestamped metrics, and a dashboard form the standard longitudinal benchmarking flow.

skills: 6.2.5: Monitoring for common training and serving errors.
questions.question:
During a production retraining run on Vertex AI custom training, a job fails partway through with a non-zero exit status. The MLOps team needs to quickly inspect stdout, stderr, and any framework-level error messages emitted by the training container.

Which is the MOST direct way to investigate?

choices.text: Open the failed training job in the Vertex AI console and follow the link to its logs in Cloud Logging, which captures the container's stdout and stderr automatically.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI training automatically streams container output to Cloud Logging, accessible directly from the failed job page.

choices.text: SSH into the training VM after the job has completed and read the local log files on the boot disk.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI custom training does not expose direct SSH into managed worker VMs and the disk is reclaimed when the job ends.

choices.text: Re-run the job with debugging disabled to see if the error reproduces.
choices.explanation: Disabling debugging reduces visibility and does not help diagnose the existing failure.

choices.text: Check Cloud Storage object access logs for the training bucket to find the error message.
choices.explanation: Storage access logs record reads and writes, not framework error messages.

questions.tip: Vertex AI integrates training output with a managed logging service.
questions.explanation:
Container logs from Vertex AI training jobs are streamed to Cloud Logging by default, and the job page links straight to them.

**Why it works:** Cloud Logging captures stdout and stderr, including framework tracebacks, making post-mortem analysis straightforward.

**Why the others don't work:**
- SSH into VM: not exposed for managed training.
- Re-running with debug off: removes visibility.
- Storage access logs: do not contain training errors.

skills: 6.2.5: Monitoring for common training and serving errors.
questions.question:
To reduce infrastructure costs, the platform team consolidated several models onto a small Vertex AI endpoint. Soon after, downstream applications begin reporting elevated 429 responses during peak traffic.

What is the MOST appropriate first response to this serving error?

choices.text: Inspect the endpoint's prediction request and replica metrics in Cloud Monitoring, then increase the minimum replica count or enable autoscaling headroom for the deployed model.
choices.explanation: 429 responses indicate throttling caused by insufficient serving capacity; scaling replicas resolves it.

choices.text: Disable Vertex AI Model Monitoring on the endpoint to free up resources.
choices.explanation: Model Monitoring sampling has minimal impact on serving capacity and disabling it removes valuable signals.

choices.text: Re-train the model with fewer features to reduce inference latency.
choices.explanation: Throttling is a capacity issue, not a model complexity issue; retraining will not resolve it.

choices.text: Move the model to BigQuery ML and serve predictions via SQL queries.
choices.explanation: Migrating to BigQuery ML is a major architectural change that does not address the immediate throttling problem on the endpoint.

questions.tip: HTTP 429 points to a specific kind of operational limit.
questions.explanation:
429 errors signal that requests are exceeding the endpoint's capacity, so the right response is to inspect serving metrics and scale.

**Why it works:** Cloud Monitoring shows whether replicas are saturated, and increasing min replicas or autoscaling headroom raises throughput so requests are no longer throttled.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disabling monitoring: not a capacity solution and reduces visibility.
- Retraining with fewer features: addresses model size, not throttling.
- Migrating to BigQuery ML: disproportionate and unrelated.

skills: 6.2.5: Monitoring for common training and serving errors.
questions.question:
The operations team is hardening observability for an online prediction service backed by Vertex AI. They want to be alerted promptly when serving errors occur and to have enough context to diagnose them.

Which TWO actions BEST achieve this with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.text: Create a Cloud Monitoring alerting policy on the prediction error rate and latency metrics for the Vertex AI endpoint.
choices.explanation: Built-in endpoint metrics are exposed to Cloud Monitoring and are the lowest-overhead way to alert on serving errors.

choices.text: Use Cloud Logging to capture endpoint request and prediction logs, with log-based metrics for specific error patterns.
choices.explanation: Cloud Logging gives the diagnostic context needed to investigate alerts raised by metrics.

choices.text: Run a continuously executing Cloud Run job that polls the endpoint and writes a custom uptime metric every second.
choices.explanation: A custom polling service duplicates managed metrics and adds operational burden.

choices.text: Disable autoscaling on the endpoint to keep error rates predictable.
choices.explanation: Disabling autoscaling tends to increase, not decrease, errors under variable load.

choices.text: Forward all prediction logs to a self-managed Elasticsearch cluster running on Compute Engine.
choices.explanation: Self-managed log search adds significant overhead compared with using Cloud Logging.

questions.tip: Look for managed observability primitives that work natively with Vertex AI endpoints.
questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring alerting on built-in metrics combined with Cloud Logging diagnostics is the lowest-overhead observability pattern.

**Why it works:** Endpoint metrics and request logs are produced automatically; you only configure alerts and log-based metrics on top of them.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Custom polling job: duplicates managed signals.
- Disabling autoscaling: makes errors more likely.
- Self-managed Elasticsearch: high operational cost.
